WORK FOR YOUNG MEN IN FOREIGN LANDS. 


DAVID McCONAUGHY FUND. 

This report covers the year ending Dec. 31, 1900, in order to 

coincide with the fiscal year of the International Committee, to whom 

this fund is reported. A new Committee has undertaken this work 

and is planning to prosecute it with greater vigour and earnestness 
amongst the members.

Through the individual gifts of five members of the Association, 
three men are sustained as Secretaries in India, and one in China, 
and one in Japan,—all of whom are engaged in work for the native 
young men of these non-Christian lands. 


Gifts towards the annual expenses of the Association, 
and also towards its extension in the city, are earnestly 
solicited by the Board of Directors, 

The Association appeals to its many friends in the 
city, for a remembrance in the final disposition of their 
property. Bequests are invited toward an Annex to the 
present Building for the enlargement of the Physical and 
Educational work, and also for special accommodation 
for work for boys; also Branch Building at Point St. 
Charles and the Northeast End; also for the develop- 
ment of the Library, and the supervision of the 
Educational work, 


ay 


ANNUAL MEETING. 


Annual Meeting of the Association was held on 
at 8.15, in the Lecture Hall, Mr. 
C. T. Williams, President, in the chair. The meeting was opened 
with devotional exercises, Mr. Budge reading the twelfth chapter of 
Romans, and Mr. J. R. Dougall leading in prayer. The minutes of 
the last Annual Meeting were read and approved. A telegram of 
congratulation was sent to the Toronto Association on the occasion 
of their Annual Meeting. 

The report of the Board of Directors was presented by Mr. D. A. 
Budge, Secretary, and the Financial Statement by Mr. L. H. Packard, 
Treasurer. Reports of the various Committees were also presented 
in regular order. On motion, the following were elected to serve 


as Directors for three years >— 


The Fiftieth 
Tuesday evening, May aith, 1901, 


D. W. Ross. J. W. Knox. G. H. Harrower. 
Cc. T. WILLIAMS. D. BENTLEY. C. E. GAUvtt. 
H. B. AMES. 


On motion of Mr. S. P. Leet, seconded by Mr. I. Gammell, the 
foliowing amendment to the By-laws of the Association was adopted: 

“Article .—Membership.—Sections 1 and 2 to read ‘Any young 
man sixteen years of age and over, and Sections 2 and 3 to read, 
‘with satisfactory references as to character and general conduct,’ 
instead of ‘ good moral character ? and Section 3 to read, ‘upon 
presentation of satisfactory evidence as to character, as above 
indicated.’ ” 

The members then listened to a stirring address from Mr. W. B. 
Millar, of the International Committee, N.Y., on the work of the 
last fifty years and the outlook for the future. 

The meeting adjourned with prayer by Mr. John Murphy, and the 
singing of “ Blest be the tie that binds.”

NNUAL REPORT OF THE BOARD OF DIRECTORS. 


_—_———_

ther in a room in the Baptist Church on St. Helen Street, 
the present time, this work for the young men of 
eal has continued without interruption. If a correct 
et of the men who have wrought out this movement in this 
+» could be made it would reach into the thousands, and 
id surely be an attractive study. A review of the past 
tory indicates the self-sacrifice and untiring labor which 
freely rendered by a large number of our predecessors, 
1 we are so greatly indebted. The majority of these 
men have passed to their reward, but they have left 
a great inheritance, and a worthy example. Let the 
ificing spirit of these early leaders fill the minds and 
of those who are now directing its affairs, so that 
er honor and glory may come to our God and greater 


¢ to our fellow young men. 


ld Power. 

ng this half century the Young Men’s Christian Asso- 
has demonstrated its right to be called “A World 
’ by its being planted in nearly every country in the 
and by its occupying almost every strategic point of 
in modern life. That young men need the prepara- 
their life work which the Association affords can no 
be questioned by any thoughtful man, and is abund- 
y proven by the constantly increasing number of young 
n who are taking advantage of the privileges offered. 


the year 1851, 


12 
Growth. 

The record of the work of the past year shows gratifying 
progress in about every Department. This is the more 
encouraging when we realize the work which is being done 
for young men throughout the city in other ways. A few 
years ago the Association was practically alone in that field, 
but now many of the churches have organizations for their 
young men, with Reading and Social Rooms, and in suburban 
sections organizations embodying the social and athletic side 
have come into existence. j 


Membership. 


The membership closed on May Ist with 2,070 young men 
and Juniors enrolled. This is the largest in our history, and 
the Committee and its Chairman, Mr. R. C. Holden, are to 
be congratulated for this result. It shows an increase of 371 
over last year. A systematic effort has been made by the 
Committee and the office towards the visitation of new 
members soon after they have joined. While this is of the 
utmost importance, the task is not an easy one when you 
consider the large number who join each month, and the diffi- 
culties of personal visitation at their homes or business. Ther 
Directors would commend the facts of the membership report 
to the careful consideration of all members. 


With Canadians in South Africa. 


This Association maintained a deep interest in the work 
of Dr. H. G. Barrie and Mr. Thos. F. Best with the Canadian 
Contingents in South Africa. Over $300 was subscribed by 
the members toward the necessary expenses, and through an 
arrangement with Miss Gould, of Montreal, the sum of $3,000 
was secured and cabled to Dr. Barrie and Mr. Best for sup- 
plying the immediate needs of the men on the field as these 
Secretaries might deem best. This was a great boon to the 
men, and it gave our representatives enlarged influence in 
the service they sought to render. The safe return of both 
Dr. Barrie and Mr. Best, after all the hardships of the cam- 


15 


is cause for devout thanksgiving to God. For the 
e record of this work see the report issued by the 


paign, 
complet 
Provincial Committee. 


Militia Camp- 

At the Militia Camp held July last at Laprairie, the Asso- 
ciation placed a tent and equipment on the field, and with 
the co-operation On Mire eel Distin, Secretary at Quebec, 
Provincial Committee and others, a good work was 
carried On- The facilities for reading, games and correspond- 
ence, and the addresses given each evening, were greatly 
appreciated by both officers and men. 


the 


Our Religious Work. 

The religious work has been animated by a helpful spirit. 
This is not confined merely to the devotional and gospel 
meetings and the Bible classes, but we strive to plan the 
whole so that there shall be no secular or religious work 
separate from each other. The religious life of the Associa- 
tion should permeate every department, and our Committee- 
men and volunteer workers should carry a religious life and 
interest into all their work. We believe this is done to a 
greater extent than ever before. As the Committee report 
will show, 4 distinct advance has been made in the all 
important matter of Bible study. We have lacked, however, 
the aggressive evangelistic effort, that reaching out after 
young men outside of our Building. We have had no special 
series of evangelistic meetings in order to bring the great 
fundamental truths of the Christian life before our men. An 
effort was made to secure this, but we were disappointed in 
not being able to get the leader. This should be remedied 
for the coming year. At least two series of such meetings 
should be held by the most competent men that can be 
secured, and more aggressive, evangelistic work undertaken 
en behalf of the young men of the city. The Directors 
suggest that this important matter have the earliest attention 
of our Religious Department Committee. 


14 
Finance. 


The financial statement will show all our bills paid at the 
close of the year. For this we are very grateful, but it shows 
a small decline in the amount of subscriptions toward current 
expenses. ‘This is accounted for in part by the greater. 
activity of the Membership Committee, who secured former 
subscribers as members, and in some cases increased their 
amount. But to meet the present and future demand of this 
magnificent field we should have a larger financial support 
from tthe citizens. The Finance Committee have plans in 
view for a more thorough canvas of the city. During the 
year one bequest was received of $450.00 from the will of 
the late Mrs. Frances A. Sanders. 


Building and Rooms. 


The Building has had careful oversight, and notwith- — 
standing the fact that its use has never been so great, your 
Directors are pleased to report that its general appearance 
is almost as attractive as when opened ten years ago. Plans 
are under consideration for some much needed improvements 
which will add to the comfort and convenience of the main 
floor. 


The Work of the Ladies’ Committee. 


The Ladies’ Committee has rendered most helpful service 
in the development of the social work and also in the appoint- 
ments of the Building. In fact, the social work in connection 
with the various departments has made great advance, so that 
the Building has become more than ever a social centre for 
the members. The work of the Ladies’ Committee has made 
this possible, and your Directors extend to them the cordial 
thanks of the Association. 


The Volunteer Working Force. 


For the detailed statement of the year’s work we, would 
refer you to the reports of the Department Committees. 
Your Directors desire to thank the chairmen and members 


15 


of Committees and all the other volunteer workers for the 
time and effort expended, and the loyal support they have 
eiven to the Board. The increase in the volunteer working 
Estce is one of the most hopeful signs for the future, as it 
offers such invaluable training for the young men who are to 
be the future leaders of the work. 


The Staff. 


The Directors desire to record their appreciation of the 
faithful service rendered by the staff, in their supervision of 
the various departments. Few of the members realize the 
multiplicity of detail, or the hours of service required in 
order to effectively supervise this large and increasing work. 
The only change in the staff was the addition of Mr. A. B. 
Dawson, as Assistant Physical Director. 


The Need of to-day is Men. 


The man of affairs to-day needs efficient men more than he 
needs anything else to enable him to carry out his projects. 
The demand for men of better training, steadier habits, higher 
character, was never greater. Young men are pushed to the 
front as never before. The colleges are filled with many who 
are making great sacrifices to secure the necessary equipment 
to meet this demand. The Association steps in to furnish this 
training, not only on the intellectual, but also on the social, 
physical and religious side of a young man’s life. It reaches 
after the great mass of employed young men. To prove that 
it is meeting this demand there are hundreds of young men 
who could give similar testimony to the writer of the follow- 
ing letter :— 

April 22, 1901. 
“Dear Mr. Bunce, 

“As you are aware, I have been identified with the Association 
oth as a junior and senior member ever since my 13th or 14th year, 
and as I have come under the influence of the work in almost all 
the branches, it seems in looking back that I have almost been 
entirely safe-guarded by those influences against the operation of 


16 


the numerous temptations which assail a young man less favorably 
situated. 
“It would be utterly impossible for me to form an estimate ¢ 
the value which my connection with the Association has been to m 
As you are aware, I have been fairly successful since entering 
commercial life, and I am convinced that the Association has be: 
andisthe greatest factor in my success. I am satisfied that ¢] 
time spent in the Association could not have been more profitab’ 
spent, and is the best investment which I could possibly have made 


Every thoughtful man must see what a tremendous respon: 
sibility thus rests upon the Association, but it can only meet 
this in proportion as it is given the enlarged means an 
facilities to carry on the work. 

Montreal is a strategic point. As a seaboard city it meets 
large numbers of young men who come to this country, J] 
is also the chief commercial city of the Dominion. The 
marked division in its population makes it a most important 
field for an organization which welcomes all young men 
character being the only test. 


Expansion in Branches. 


At no single point can the work be accomplished. Other 
cities like Buffalo, Pittsburg, New York and Chicago have 
met this need by Branches, all directed by a central Board, 
New York City has eighteen Branches, and others are bein 
added each year. These Branches need not be as large or 
expensive as the Central Building, but they should be adapted 
to the locality. A careful study of the map compiled by thi 
Membership Committee, showing where each membe 
resides, clearly indicates the sections of the city which need 
to be covered, These are 


Point St. Charles. Annex to Central Building, 
The North-East End. with separate Boys’ Department, 
French Branch in East End Evening Class Rooms, 


Addition to the Gymnasium. 

We had hoped to be able to report the beginning of the | 
Point St. Charles Branch, but matters hate arisen causing 
delay. We trust that these will be cleared away soon, and 


17 


y needed, begun. Our growth in this 
ilding and any marked increase in several of the depart- 
eS i well nigh impossible without enlargement. This 
J source of great concern to the Directors. 

The importance of a separate equipment for the Boys’ 
yenartment is most urgent. The business boys are a large 
jncreasing class, and we can practically do nothing more 
or them with our present equipment unless we conflict with 
Swork of the young men. For this special department, 
. York, Cleveland, Brooklyn, and other cities, are 
e rooms and buildings. We must do the 
t the demands and provide for the 


, Branch, so greatl 


iding separat 
ne if we are to mee 
a 

‘Superior Opportunity for Investment. 

Most wealthy men of to-day started poor. They have 
‘wht their way to success in this hard battle of life. They 
place a high estimate on those agencies which enable 
oung men to rise by means of wise and helpful use of their 
sure time. We do not believe that any investment can be 
made by our citizens either by gift or bequest which would 
have a more beneficent or far-reaching influence than in an 
ency of this kind which is moulding the lives of the boys 
and young men, who in coming years will control the com- 
mercial and public interests of the city and country. The 
Directors earnestly commend this to the consideration of all 
public-spirited citizens and persons of larger means. 


Prayer the Power. 


A review of the past history of our Association shows the 
important place which prayer has ever occupied. Those in 
charge have realized this to be a sacred trust committed to 
them by God, and have sought His guidance and help in its 
_ prosecution. Whenever new plans have been presented they 
have been committed to God for counsel, “ For unless the 
Lord build the house they labor in vain that build it.” This 
has been pre-eminently true the past year. Each Friday 


18 


morning at 8.30 the Directors have met for prayer on beha] 
of the work. These prayers have been abundantly answere 
Let the Association be encouraged to go forward int 
Twentieth Century to still greater achievements. a 


In Memoriam. 


During the past year death has made great havoc in ov 
ranks. Our men are falling by the way, reminding us th 
whatever good thing we plan to do must be done quickly, ; 
our opportunities may be gone. Some of these have bee 
valued friends of the Association for many years.

e action of the Board of Directors in tendering every Montreal 
er on his return from South Africa a year’s membership ticket 
, was highly appreciated, and 61 men took advantage of the offer. 


24 


The Committee, although unable to personally attend the Kingston 
Convention last February, were able to send up their Secretary to 
represent them and report on his return. 

The Committee strongly felt the need of some suitable sign on 
our building. They were very glad, through the generous help of 
a number of friends, to be able without demand upon the Associa- 
tion Treasury, to place over the front door, the sign which now by 
day and night tells every passer-by the purpose of our fine building. 

The Committee have just provided a new means of studying the 
membership problem, in the shape of a large map of the city, upon 
which is marked out the home addresses of our entire membership, 
its special purpose being to prove what sections of the city we 
influence from our present headquarters, and at what points our first 
Branch Associations are most needed. 

We close, asking the continued co-operation of our members in 
making men acquainted with the privileges our building offers and 
in securing them as members. 


Respectfully submitted, 
RUFUS C. HOLDEN, 


Chairman.

REPORTS OF COMMITTEES. 


RELIGIOUS AND BIBLE STUDY DEPARTMENT. 


One of the chief features of the work of this department during 
the year was its reorganization at the beginning of the season in 
the effort to co-relate the various meetings and religious agencies 
of the Association under one general department Committee. This 
Committee has met regularly each month, usually on the first 
Thursday, for the consideration of reports from the Sub-Committees, 
and has taken united action upon all matters affecting the religious 
life and work of the Association. This effort to bring the religious 
work of the Association under one Committee has been successful 
and promises greater things for the future. The Sub-Committees 
report as follows :— 


YOUNG MEN’S MEETING. 


This meeting has been held every Saturday evening during the 
year, with an average attendance of 50, the same as last year. While 
the meeting runs considerably over this number during the fall and 
winter, in the summer months the attendance falls below, largely 
due, the Committee believe, to the absence from the city, on Saturday 
afternoon and evening of many, as a result of the general half-holiday 
during the summer months. The Committee, after earnest and care- 
ful discussion, suggest that the meeting be held on Thursday evening 
for the months of June, July and August. The meeting has been a 
source of great help and blessing to many. Conversation has been 
had with enquiriers nearly every week at the close of the meetings, 
and the invitation has been given regularly in connection with the 
meeting to those desirous of beginning the Christian life. The 
meeting has also been a training to many by taking part in personal 
testimony and words of comment upon the subject for the evening. 
Many young men have here received a development in Christian 
Bae vice which has fitted them for larger responsibilities in Christian 
work. 


MEN’S MEETING. 


This meeting was held on Sunday afternoon at 4.15, from October 
28th to April 28th, with a total attendance of 3,105, and an average 
attendance of 115. Special vocal music was arranged for nearly every 
meeting. The sticcess of the past winter’s work proves that there 
is a place for this meeting and that it is needed. Many have 
attended who do not come to any other religious meeting in the 
Association. The special features of the year were addresses by Dr. 
Barrie, on his return from South Africa; by Rey. Wm. Sparling and 
Rev. Dean Carmichael, at the Memorial Service of our late 
Sovereign ; and J. Campbell White, of Calcutta, India. With these 
exceptions all our speakers were from the city. Special mention 
should be made of the very interesting series of addresses in January 
reviewing the Nineteenth Century and forecasting the Twentieth in 


97 


ai 


its special bearing upon the religious life of young men. We are 
also deeply grateful to Prof. H. M. Tory, who gave a series of seven 
addresses on the general theme of ‘‘ What the coming of Jesus Christ 
to the World has meant to the Life and Thought of Men.” These 
were all a strong presentation of the truth and helpful and stimulat- 
ing to those who heard them. 


BIBLE STUDY DEPARTMENT. 


The Committee in charge of this work carefully planned a course 
of studies for the fall and winter months, and early in September 
issued a neat prospectus to members and others. A Bible Study 
Rally was held on Saturday evening, October 13th, which did much 
to interest men in the classes. These commenced October 16th, and 
met weekly on Tuesday evening, from seven to eight, until April 
30th. Tea was provided at the Building from 6.30 to 7.00 for those 
attending, at a cost of ten cents, which was appreciated both for the 
convenience and for the social intercourse enjoyed by the members 
of the classes. The following is a statement of the leaders and 
attendance at all classes :—

The thanks of the Committee and Association are due to Prof. 
Ross, and also to Mr. A. M. MacKay for their kindness in conducting 
their classes during the season. 


YOUNG MEN’S BIBLE CLASS. 


The average attendance at the class for the past year was 66, 
making a total attendance for the year of 3,451, being an increase 
of 789 compared with the previous year. During the season the class 
made a study of “ Twenty-five Important Decisions,” followed by 
“The Lives of Prominent men-in the Bible,” which has been of much 
interest and profit to the members. A Xmas Service was held on 
Sunday, December 23rd, when we were kindly assisted by Mrs. 
Budge, Messrs. J. S. Penman and A. Nettleship. Personal calls 
were made and flowers sent on several occasions to sick members. 


28 


The class appointed Mr. Wm. Young as a delegate to the Kingston 
Convention. The Annual Class Tea was held on Sunday, February 
24th, at which 113 men were present. Short addresses were given 
by Mr. T. C. Williams and Mr. L. H. Packard, which were much 
enjoyed. The thanks of the Committee are due to the Ladies’ Com- 
mittee for their kindness in preparing and serving the tea. Thanks 
are also due to the following gentlemen who conducted the class in 
the absence of Mr. Budge :—Rev. J. Gordon, Rev. Dr. Lawson, Rev. 
Dr. Johnston, Dr. Rutherford, N. Kobayashi, of Tokio, Japan, and 
C. K. Calhoun. 

We earnestly hope the members will make the class known as 
much as possible, so that more men may be benefited. 


HOSPITAL. 


The Western Hospital Committee report their work in a most 
satisfactory condition. Service is held in the wards of the hospital 
every Sunday morning. They have upwards of a dozen workers. 
engaged in this work, and desire to thank the ladies of Mountain 
Street Methodist Church Choir and Erskine Church Y.P.S.C.E., who 
sc ably assist with the music on alternate Sundays. Our thanks. 
are also due to the officials in the hospital whose hearty sympathy 
has been accorded throughout the year. That our work has been 
appreciated is evident from the many words of thanks received from 
the patients. We trust and pray that God will continue to bless the 
efiorts of the Committee during the coming year. 


G. H. HARROWER, 
Chairman. 


SOCIAL DEPARTMENT. 


In addition to the regular events, the Committee arranged for two 
new features this past season, as follows :— 

On St. Andrew’s night a Scotch Concert was given in Associa- 
tion Hall, which was largely attended. An admission fee of 25 cents, 
was charged and excellent talent provided. Our aim was to provide 
a first-class concert at a low cost, and many of the members availed 
themselves of the opportunity. It proved a success in every way. 

On March 7th we held an “At Home” to members and their lady 
friends, the idea being to provide an evening similar to a home 
gathering, with games, music, recitations and refreshments. About 
75 were present. It proved so successful that another was held on 
. April 23rd on a larger scale, and despite the unfavorable weather, 
over 100 attended. The members were invited alphabetically. It is 
hoped this feature may continue another year. 

On the evening of Thanksgiving Day we did not forget the young 
men away from home and prepared for them a supper. Over 60 sat 
down to the inviting tables, kindly provided and waited upon by the 
Ladies’ Committee. The usual toasts were proposed and responded” 
to, This supper is always heartily appreciated by the young men. 


29 


Our Annual Reception on New Year’s Day was a decided success. 
The Building was taxed to its utmost by visitors. Among the many 
attractions provided were the exhibition by the Physical Depart- 
ment in the Gymnasium, the Biograph views of the Grand Trunk 
Railway System and the South African war souvenirs. The Camera 
Club’s exhibit this year was exceptionally fine, and the excellence 
oi their work was much commented on. The usual evening concert 
was given in Association Hall. Illustrated views of Japan were 
shown in the Lecture Hall by our ex-President, Alderman H. B. 
Ames. The Association Orchestra furnished music in the afternoon 
and evening, and the ladies served refreshments in the Lecture Hall. 
The New Year’s Reception is always most enjoyable and is looked 
forward to by old and new members each year. 


THE STRANGERS’ TEA. 


Committee report having held eleven Sunday evening Teas during 
the year, with an average attendance of 30. Much the same plan 
has been carried on as in former years. One new feature is worthy 
oi mention. At least one of the Ladies’ Committee has been present 
at each of the Teas, giving the occasion a more home-like feeling. 
We take this opportunity of thanking the Ladies’ Committee for the 
assistance they have so kindly rendered us at all times, not only by 
their presence at the Teas, but also in the supplying of refreshments. 

For the benefit of those who may not be acquainted with this 
Committee, we would say that these Teas are held at 5.15 on Sunday 
evenings about once a month, to which are invited strangers in 
Montreal whom the Committee have learned of. Our object is to 
have them become acquainted with the Association and its work, and 
with one another. In this way many agreeable as well as helpful 
acquaintances have been formed, and we are encouraged by the 
results which have followed. Efforts are also made to introduce 
them to churches of their choice. 


THE EVENING RECEPTION COMMITTEE 


has had members on duty in the evenings on the reception floor 
throughout the year as faithfully as possible. The records show that 
over 255 strangers coming from Great Britain and_ Ireland, 


30 


Australia, South America, United States and our own country, have 
visited the Building and been welcomed by the members of the 
Committee. The Committee has also been instrumental in securing 
at least 30 new members for the Association during the year. In the 
summer and early fall a number of informal parlor entertainments 
were arranged for, which proved very enjoyable, and interested a 
large number of young men. The members of the Committee have 
assisted at various social entertainments during the year, and have 
been of assistance to the office when required, during the specially 
busy evenigs of October and November. 


ALEX. ARTHUR, 


Chairman. 


EDUCATIONAL DEPARTMENT. 


Instruction was given during the past season in 14 different 
subjects, with a view to rendering the utmost practical assistance to 
young men employed during the day. In 6 of these subjects instruc- 
tion was given in both elementary and advanced grades. Twenty- 
three classes were held, 6 meeting once a week, and 17 twice a week, 
making a total of 40 classes each week. 

Four hundred and two individual students entered the classes, with 
a total enrolment of 578 (some students taking more than one class) 
being a gain of 55 per cent. over last year. 

It became necessary to divide the Elementary French class after 
the season opened, owing to its size, and Mr. F. de Repentigny was 
engaged to teach the extra class. The sessions of the German class 
were increased from three-quarters of an hour to one hour each, 
The Advanced class in English was replaced this year by a course 
in English literature, under Mr. I. Gammell, B.A. Shakespeare’s 
“Merchant of Venice” and “ Hamlet” were studied. Ladies intro- 
duced by members of the Association were admitted to this class. 
The Isaac Pitman system of Phonography was taught this season, 
and an Advanced class added. A class in Algebra and Geometry 
was added to the curriculum for the benefit of the students in 
Electricity. It was found, however, that the students entering varied 
very much in their knowledge of Mathematics, and some better plan 
will have to be adopted for another season. A class in Elementary 
Architectural Drawing was added this year. While it was not large, 
yet the interest and attendance was above the average. New classes 
were also held in Electricity and Commercial Law. The latter class 
proved very popular and useful among young business men. 

The other classes were carried on as formerly. Students are 
required to be full members of the Association, and to pay a small 
tuition fee. Sustaining members were exempt from fees. 

Seventy different students wrote on the International Examina- 
tions conducted in Arithmetic, Stenography, English, Electricity, 
Bookkeeping, and Mechanical Drawing. Forty-one of these have 
been passed by the teaching staff and their papers sent to the Inter-” 
national Board of Examiners, New York City. 


ol 


Of this number thirty-five were granted certificates by the Interna- 

tional Board, as follows :— 

English, Elementary.—F. Slocombe, 85; A. Weir, 75; J. W. Weir, 75. 

Arithmetic, Elementary.—D. Wright, 8o. 

Arithmetic, Advanced.—J. Atter, 95; H. Stafford, 92: H. T. Owens, 
80; W. H. Whinfield, 79; L. Willows, 75. 

Mechanical Drawing, Elementary.—F. 8B. Kilbourn, 92; W. J. 
Phillips, 89; A. S. Richardson, 80; D. Angus, 78. 

Mechanical Drawing, Advanced.—H. W. Meyers, 80; J. W. Buckland, 
80; B. R. Deacon, 77; E. Duckett, 75. 

Electricity, Elementary.—S. McOuat, 86; A. A. Owens, 77. 

Bookkeeping, Elementary.—H. Stafford, 100; Walter Lauer, 84; 
H. T. Somers, 83; T. S. Trenaman, 83. 

Bookkeeping, Advanced.—H. H. Hopkins, 94; F. R. Yule, 93; E. L. 
Miles, 92; F. A. Crowe, 88; R. E. Dixon, 88; W. J. Marshall, 84; 
J. W .Carlyle, 82; E. E. Hamilton, 77. 

Stenography, Advanced.—J. McKeen, 98; E. C. Budge, 95; J. H. 
Taylor, 80; D. E. McIntyre, 80. 


Special attention was given to the social side of the educational 
work with gratifying results. The opening Educational Rally, 
usually held the latter part of September, or the first week of October, 
took place this year on December 6th, after the classes had got well 
under way. It was attended by about 400 of the students and their 
friends, and was more strictly an educational gathering than any 
of the receptions heretofore. The programme consisted of an 
address to the students by our President, Mr. C. T. Williams, music 
and refreshments. Early in the season steps were taken to form 
what afterwards became an educational league. This is a group of 
students, consisting of a Chairman and Secretary elected from each 
class, forming a student body representative of all our evening 
classes. It resulted in the students of the various classes becoming 
better acquainted and contributing valuable suggestions as to the 


conduct of the work as a whole. The closing event of the season 
was our Educational Supper on Thursday evening, April 18th, at 
which 140 students, teachers and committeemen were present. 
Excellent addresses were given by Messrs. H. B. Ames, Henry 
Miles, Prof. H. M. Tory, A. M. MacKay, Isaac Gammell, and others. 
Great interest in our evening class work was developed, and we 
believe that its result on next season’s work will be very consider- 
able. Increased class room accommodation is urgently needed for 
the future of the work. It must be remembered also that the cost 
oi the classes is paid, year by year, from the current revenue, so that 
it is impossible to hold classes in any given subject unless a sufficient 
attendance is secured to cover a certain proportion of the cost. 
We could reach a great many more men had we an endowment of 
some kind which would enable us to hold classes for smaller groups 
of men. This becomes a necessity, as subjects are graded to meet 
the needs of advanced students, 
A statement of the class attendance is given herewith :—

The following are extracts from letters received from last year’s 
students :— 

“T have attended the evening classes for the past three years, and 
the practical knowledge acquired has been of the greatest value to 
me. I have always found the teaching well adapted to the varied 
needs of commercial life, and have no hesitation in saying that there 
is no more helpful institution in Montreal for young men who wish 
to increase their efficiency than the Educational Department of the 
Y.M.C.A. It is to be commended in the first place because the 
subjects taught are those best suited for young men, and, secondly, 
because its advantages are within the reach of all. 

‘Wishing you every success, I am,’ 


“T cannot pass without speaking of the many benefits received 
through attendance at the Y.M.C.A. Educational classes, my chief 
regret being that I did not take advantage of them long ago. I 
believe their usefulness to young men engaged in mercantile life 
cannot be overestimated, and any who neglect the opportunities for 
improvement thus offered are doing themselves a great injustice. I 
can certainly commend them to any young man as a first- class means 
of overcoming any deficiencies in his school training..’ 


A. M. MACKAY, 
Ghairman. 


READING ROOM AND LIBRARY. 


There is no part of our Building so largely used as our Reading 
Room, not only by our members, but by visitors and strangers, and 
it is the constant aim of the Committee to keep it thoroughly abreast 
of the times. 

There are 148 periodicals on the tables and files, 37 being donated 
by the publishers and friends, and the balance paid for by the Com- 
mittee at a cost of $241.92. The following new periodicals have 
been added to the list :— 


Black and White, Fliegenden Blatter, 
Canadian Architect and Builder, Chicago Record, 
British Monthly, Musical Opinion, 
Photographic Times, Musical Herald. 


A few of the better class magazines have been kept on the tables 
in the parlors. This has been appreciated by our members, as the 
parlor is a comfortable place to spend a quiet social hour. Our sale 
of magazines and papers took place late in December and realized 
$78.33. The sale next year will be held on the first Thursday in 
December. 

The Library is being used to a greater extent every succeeding 
year. The number of books given out during ihe year was 7,665, as 
compared with 5,667 the preceding year. Of this number 69 per 
cent. was fiction, 5 per cent. religious, 6 per cent history, 2 per cent. 
travel, 2 per cent. biography, 7 per cent. science, 2 per cent. poetry, 
I per cent. social and political, and 6 per cent. miscellaneous. Seven 
hundred and seventeen members have used the Library, as compared 
with 638 last year. There are now 3,905 volumes in the Library. One 
hundred and sixty-five have been added during the year. 


34 


The following are a few of the most popular books with our 
readers at present :—Eben Holden, Janice Meredith, Richard Carvel, 
Soldiers of Fortune, In the Palace of the King, Black Rock, Sky 
Pilot, Alice of Old Vincennes, Heart of the Ancient Wood, Seats of 
the Mighty, Chien D’Or, Les Miserables, Wild Animals I have 
known, Royal Manhood, How England saved Europe,, The Great 
Boer War, From London to Ladysmith via Pretoria, The Habitant, 
Great Books as Life Teachers, Forty-one years in India. 

Donations of books, or money to buy books, will be gratefully 
received. The usefulness of the Library would be greatly 
increased by a reclassification of all the books and the instituting 
of the card system of cataloguing; in fact this is very much needed. 
It is hoped that we will be able to obtain the necessary funds to do 
this during the present summer. 

I. GAMMELL, 


Chairman. 


CAMERA CLUB. 


Meetings have been held regularly, and the membership has 
increased considerably. It has been quite a successful year, as has 
been shown by the fine exhibits of work. The exhibition given in 
the Board Room on New Year's Day would have done credit to 
any photographic show rooms in the city, and this was one of the 
most popular points of interest in the New Year's Day reception. A 
collection of about forty photographs was sent to the Kingston 
Convention Exhibit, and it is needless to say that it compared favor- 
ably with the exhibits from other Associations. Another collection 
is in course of preparation for the Boston Jubilee Convention in June. 
We hope to do ourselves credit there also. 

A Competition was held among the members of the club during 
the winter, and the number of entries was larger than any previous 
year. The judges mentioned that the work was of an unusually high 
order for amateur work. The thanks of the club are due Mr. 
George Barratt and Mr. A. I. Rice for prizes given by them. The 
studio and dark rooms have been well used. ‘The former has been 
greatly improved, especially by the addition of a large back ground, 
the gift of Mr. Rice. These rooms are accessible at any time to the 
club members by applying at the office for the keys. 


H. W. WELLER, 
Chairmane. 


PHYSICAL DEPARTMENT. 


In reviewing the work of the past year, we are pleased to be able 
to report the interest in the various divisions of this department well 
sustained, and the work in all the clubs satisfactory. Last year, Mr. 
George E. Winter resigned his position as Assistant Physical 
Director, and the duties of that office were assumed by Mr. A. B. 
Dawson, who during the past year has rendered most efficient service. 
All the clubs have closed their year in good financial standing, the 
accounts of two balance exactly, while the remaining seven show a 
credit balance varying from 42 cents to $47.15. 


Or 
vo 


In connection with the general work of the Physical Department, 
it seems fitting that the present should record the step taken in con- 
nection with League Games. Some weeks ago, through the Physical 
Committee, an application was made to the Directorate for permis- 
sion to enter League games. This application, which once again 
raised the question now some years in abeyance, was dealt with by 
the Board with the greatest of consideration, and it was with much 
pleasure that the reply was received, granting permission under 
certain conditions for the Baseball Club to enter the League. 

At the beginning of the year Dr. W. F. Hamilton resigned his 
position as examiner in the Gymnasium Department, and was suc- 
ceeded by Dr. F. W. Gilday. To Drs. W. S. Morrow and F. W. 
Gilday the thanks of the Committee are due for the service so 
efficiently rendered. 

Another matter which comes out of a careful review and com- 
parison of the figures denoting the attendance in the Gymnasium 
Classes during the last ten years, is the general marked improvement 
in the regularity of attendance on the classes throughout the year. 
This, we think, indicates that there is a more fixed purpose on the 
part of those entering upon the autumn work, and at the same time 
proves the greater acceptableness and efficiency of the work. 


LEADERS’ CORPS. 
PEGE: eee es... EE PDE Nes ICETDS 


The Leaders’ Corps has framed its Constitution and had it printed 
with the By-Laws of the Physical Department. This step seems to 
be already warranted by the numerous demands for this constitution 
from many other Associations throughout Canada, the United 
States and Ireland. 

The members enrolled in this corps number twenty-four. 

Your Committee appreciate the faithful services rendered by the 
Leaders, and it is felt that their co-operation with the Physical 
Director is indispensable. Our most cordial thanks are hereby 
extended to them.

The interest in the Bicycle Club has been fully sustained. The 
social side of the members’ life was developed through the hospitality 
shown to this club, and many pleasant recollections gather round the 
outings. The club closed the year with a small balance to its credit. 


THE BOWLING ALLEY. 


The bowling alleys were thoroughly renovated at the beginning 
of the season, which opened on the 14th of November, and closed 
on the 27th of April. It has been a very satisfactory one in regard 
to the attendance of the bowlers on the alleys, and the club closes the 
year with a balance of $47.15 in the treasury.

TENNIS CLUB. 
Presidents) GR, :. 0." ce Renee WEL SHARE: 


The membership is 37. The club played three other tennis clubs in 
a series of games, winning third place. The ensuing year promises 
to be one of increased activity and interest, on account of the new 
arrangements entered into last autumn, by which the vacant ground 
about the Western Hospital was secured. Thus five courts will be 
provided. This club also, while under considerable expense, closed 
the year with some balance in the treasury.

membership during the past year has numbered 30. Four matches 
were played with other teams, all of which resulted in decided victory 
for the club. The balance is on the right side.

want felt by this club. It is believed that the Annual Field Day, held 
September 27th, was one of the most successful ever held by the 
Association, the attendance being much larger than usual. There 
were 130 entries for about 65 men. The liberality of the friends of 
the Athletic Club in providing the prizes is hereby gratefully acknow- 
ledged. The balance to the credit of the club is $3.00.

JUNIOR DEPARTMENT, 


In presenting the report of the past season’s work your Com- 
mittee feel that there is cause for great thankfulness to God for the 
measure of success which has attended the department throughout 
another year, and realize, as never before, the importance of the 
work as they have come into contact with the increasing number 
of boys who are availing themselves of the privileges offered for 
self-improvement. The statistics given below will show to what 
extent these privileges have been used. 

RELIGIOUS.—The Boys’ Meeting has been conducted each 
Friday night and has been a great help to the Christian boys, while 
many who did not profess to be Christians have taken a definite 
stand for Christ. 

Six sessions of the Boys’ Rally were held on Sunday afternoon, 

A service of song has been conducted in the General Hospital 
on the first Sunday of each month. 

Two Bible Training Classes have met regularly throughout the 
season. The “ Life of Christ” was taught by Mr. Wm. Young, and 
“ Bible Heroes” by Mr. John Brown. 

The money subscribed through the Missionary boxes will be 
spent in the interests of the work for boys in India. 


EDUCATIONAL.—The holding of evening classes for Business 
Boys was a new feature of the department. The large enrolment and 
faithful attendance of the students has shown the wisdom of this 
step. Should the accommodation be provided the Committee believe 
that this branch of the work will grow to very large proportions 
within the next few years. 

Additions have been made to the Library from time to time, and 
the number of periodicals in the Reading Room has been increased. 

SOCIAL.—The Social work has been maintained throughout the 
year. Special mention should be made of the Opening and Closing 
Entertainments, Illustrated Lecture by Mr. John Currie, and the 
Annual Sleigh Drive. The Closing Entertainment was largely 
attended, numbering upwards of 530, including parents and boys. 
All day outings and snowshoe tramps have also added interest to 
this phase of the work. 

Much has been added to the attractiveness of the rooms by their 
being retinted, and your Committee feel sure the members will one 
and all show their appreciation of this by doing all they can to keep 
them in their present condition. 

PHYSICAL.—Great interest has been manifested in the Gym- 
nasium Classes and they have been well attended. 

The “Tom Thumb” and “ Giant Killers” Basket ball Tourna- 
ments have been conducted successfully, keen competition being 
displayed in each series. Photographs of the winning teams, the 
“Stars” and “ Vics.” were taken. A photograph was also taken of 
the School Boys’ “ Gymnasium Class Leaders.” 

THE JUNIOR CAMP was held from 28th June to r4th July. As 
hitherto, it was most successful, and the Committee are looking 
forward to this year’s camp with even brighter prospects. 

COMMITTEE WORK.—Faithful and conscientious work has 


been performed by the 45 boys who served on the various 
Committees. 


39 


The Committee regret the withdrawal from active service of 
Mr. R. B. Ross, Jr., late Chairman of the department, who removed 
from the city. 

The Committee would like to testify to the diligent and earnest 
work of Mr. John Brown, who has had the supervision of the 
department during the year, 

The following figures show the average attendance at the various 
meetings and classes :—

PERMANENT CAMP COMMITTEE, 


Every year witnesses a great increase of interest in our camp, as 
well as a larger number of members attending. 1900 breaks all 
former records. 


The Juniors had the use of the club house from July 1st to July 
14th. Fifty-two took advantage of camp privileges last season, as 
against 37 the year before ; of the former number 41 were out for full 
length of time. There were an unusual number of rainy days during 
the two weeks, but this did not dampen their enthusiasm. 

Receipts from Junior camp were $441.23, expenditure $433.32, 
leaving a balance on hand of $7.01. 

The Senior Department handled two parties, one in May, the other 
in September, last year, in addition to the regular summer season, 
which extended from July 14th to September 4th. It was without 
doubt the best year in the camp’s history, as is shown by the follow- 
ing figures. Total receipts from Senior Camp were $1,175.99 ; 
disbursements, $1,175.99; expenses, $1,190.05; balance due Permanent 
Camp Committee, $14.06. 


Your Committee beg to report as follows :— 


42 
RAILROAD DEPARTMENT, POINT ST. CHARLES. 


In reviewing the work of the year I have endeavored to give you 
as clear and exact a report as possible; but, while at present we are 
carrying on a good work, our equipment and premises will not admit 
of our extending or enlarging it. God is certainly blessing the work 
among the railroad men, as is manifested by the several conversions 
during the year, and we have every reason to render Him our 
sincere thanks. The railway men are certainly showing their appre- 
ciation of our endeavors to furnish them with a good home away 
from home, by the large numbers who have applied for membership, 
and whom we have had to turn away owing to lack of room. Our 
united prayers are that God will in His loving kindness open up the 
way for us, and that this long looked for new building will soon 
be an established fact. 


MEMBERSHIP.—Our membership on May Ist, 1900, was 149, 
and on April 30th, 1901, was 163, showing an increase of 14 members, 
made up of 131 railroad men and 32 others. During the year 27 
members have withdrawn or removed, most of them, however, trans- 
ferred to other Associations. 


DAILY VISITS.—The total number of visits to the rooms during 
the year was 29,581, a daily average of 83. 

MEETINGS.—The attendance at our Saturday night Men’s 
meetings was 735, average weekly attendance, 14. This number 
should be more, as no meetings were held during the months of 
August and September. 

MR. BLACKALLER’S BIBLE CLASS.—Two months ago, our 
Chairman, Mr. Blackaller, started a Men’s Topical Bible Class, and 
during the past four of five meetings the smallest number we had was 
18. At our last meeting there were 32 men present. 


SUNDAY MORNING CLASS.—The Sunday morning Bible 
Class, held from 9.30 to 10.30, led by the Secretary, is also meeting 
with success. The attendance during the year was 402, average 8. 

SUNDAY AFTERNOON MEETING.—Our Sunday afternoon 
Meetings, held at 4.15 for railroad men, their families and friends, 
has proved to be one of the best features of our work. During the 
past two or three months we have had repeatedly to turn people 
away. The attendance during the past twelve months, 4,462, 
average, 86. 

MEN’S SUNDAY TEA MEETING.—On the second Sunday of 
each month, the Women’s Auxiliary, at the close of the afternoon 
service, invite all the railroad men running into Montreal whose 
homes are not in the city, to remain and have supper with us. The 
average attendance at these meetings was 19. 


BATHS.—The number of baths taken during the year was 1,788, 
daily average, 5. We have two tub baths, and one shower, with hot 
and cold water. 

REST ROOMS.—During the twelve months, 4,311 men have 
used our rest rooms, average, 12. As we have only 10 beds, you will 
see that we have slept two more each night than we have beds for. 
In our Association it is a case of first come, first served. This will 
show the need of larger premises. . 


LUNCH ROOM.—Our kitchen, where there is a gas stove 


45 


provided for the men to cook their meals, is much used, as a great 
number of the men carry their food with them. 


HOSPITAL WORK.—Eight hundred and seventy-three sick and 
injured men were visited during the year by our Hospital Committee. 
Mr. Thomas Davis, the convener, deserves special mention for his 
unfailing and ever faithful attention to this important duty. Our 
ambulance and emergency hospital room was used 24 times during 
the year, average, twice a month. 


SOCIALS.—We have had several enjoyable socials, one of the 
best being the Farewell Social and Presentation to Mr. Morrison. 
The enjoyable part was not in the fact of Mr. Morrison’s going 
away, but in the good time enjoyed by all. Mr. Morrison was 
presented by the Directors with a handsome travelling case, while 
the members presented him with a “ bureau” trunk. In presenting 
Mr. Morrison with the trunk, Mr. Sam. Pugh, in the name of the 
Association, wished Mr. Morrison all possible success in his new 
field. Mr. Morrison left Montreal at the end of September, having 
received and accepted a call to the Association at Concord, N.H. 
Another enjoyable Social was the Annual Supper, at which a 
presentation was made to Miss Blackaller, who acted as organist for 
our Association ever since its inception four years ago. 


CONCERT.—On October 30th, we held our first Annual Concert 
in the Hall of the Grand Trunk Reading Room and Scientific 
Institute. This was a grand success. After paying all expenses we 
had a balance in our favor of $65.00. 


NEW YEAR’S DAY.—On New Year’s Day we held open house 
all day, the ladies assisting in decorating the rooms, providing 
refreshments, etc. We had over 200 callers, and in the evening were 
packed to overflowing and had a most enjoyable concert. 


THE WOMEN’S AUXILIARY.—The Women’s Auxiliary is one 
of the most flourishing branches of our Association. Mrs. W. H. 
Mingie is President, Miss Lucy White, Secretary, and Miss Mingie, 
Treasurer. The ladies have always shown a deep interest in our 
work, and we have great pleasure in testifying to the helpful work they 
have rendered, not only in looking after our temporal requirements, 
but also our spiritual wants. They have always been equally willing 
to assist the Treasurer when called upon, and after helping us sub- 
stantially during the year, they have been able to carry forward a 
balance of $51.00.

IN CONCLUSION. 


A word about Life Assurance. It is both Protection and 
Investment. Nothing protects so securely as a policy in a reliable 
Assurance Company like the Sun Life of Canada,—as regards invest- 
ment, many people say this ““ Prosperous and Progressive’? Company 
is a leader. Here is an extract from a letter recently received from 
Mr. D. H. Maclaren, a prominent druggist of Barrie, Ont.:— 


* Being a firm believer in life assurance, I carry policies in the 
three leading Canadian companies and one in an American company, 
but I have always received larger profits from the Sun Life of 
Canada than from any other company. A short time ago I had a 
15-year Endowment with accrued profits matured in another Canadian 
company for $2,000, and upon the $2,000 for the same period, the 
profits were almost identical as I received on $1,000 in the Sun Life 
of Canada. This is a fair comparison, and shows why I lately took 
$2,000 more assurance in the Sun Life Assurance Company of 
Canada. I might also state that the amount received on my policy 
just matured is more than the agent with whom I placed the assur- 
ance told me it would likely amount to.” 


It may be worth your while to keep in touch with the Sun Life of 
Canada. Sunshine, the Company's monthly, is on the Y.M.C. A® 
Reading Room table. It will keep you posted. 


ADDRESSES, JUBILEE CELEBRATION, JUNE 8-10, 1901. 


The fiftieth anniversary of the organization of the Young 
Men’s Christian Association in the City of Montreal was 
celebrated by a series of Jubilee meetings on June 8, 9, and 
10, as follows:— 

On Saturday night, June 8th, at 7.45 o’clock, in Association 
Hall, an opening song service was conducted by Mr. J. 
Ritchie Bell, after which Mr. L. H. Packard took the chair. 
The hall was well filled with Association members and their 
friends, including many prominent delegates from Great 
Britain, United States and Canada, who had come to partici- 
pate in the meetings. 

On the platform were seated: Messrs. F. E. Grafton, P. 
W. Wood and David Bentley, Charter members ; Messrs. 
Geo. Brush, J. R. Dougall, Charles Alexander, Henry 
Morton, Jas. Ross, Joseph Rielle, John Murphy, and other 
early officers and committeemen, besides representatives from 
Great Britain, the United States and Canada. 

The meeting opened with the singing of the Doxology, 
and the hymn, “ O, God, our help in ages past,” after which 
Rev. J. A. Gordon, of the First Baptist Church, read the 
Scriptures and led in prayer. 


Mr. L. H. Packarp, Chairman, said :-— 


“We are here to-night to thank God for all His mercies during 
the last fifty years which have passed away, never to be recalled 
except in memory. As we look back we see how, year after year, 
His guiding hand has brought us thus far on the way, and has so 
blessed and honored the Association that we cannot but feel that the 
most devoted, earnest and practical way we could have of celebrat- 
ing our Jubilee to-night would be simply in a season of prayer and 
supplication and praise. But we have here with us so many 
friends who have come to share with us in this rejoicing upon our 
prosperity, through God, that I know you will have pleasure in 
meeting and hearing them.” 


Mr. C. K. Calhoun, Assistant Secretary, read a number of 
letters from the following gentlemen expressing regret that 


46 


it was impossible for them to be present at this Jubilee 
Celebration :—Messrs. James Stokes, New York City; F. M. 
Pratt, Toronto; Robt. Kilgour, Toronto; F. W. Ober, 
Editor “Association Men,” Chicago ; Geo. E. Williams, St. 
John, N.B.; Geo. A. Coxhead, St. Louis; L. W. Messer, 
Chicago ; W. H. Morriss, Baltimore, Md.; and others. 


Mr. C. T. Wretiams, President, welcomed the visitors as 
follows :— 


“T feel proud to be introduced as President of the Montreal 
Young Men’s Christian Association. It is an honor to any man in 
this city, or even if he came from another, but when I think that 
this is our fifty years Jubilee, and when I listen to such letters as 
those which have just been read, and hear of the interest and the 
work which has always been done by Montreal, I feel like Jamie in 
the ‘Bonnie Briar Bush.” We have met here together that we 
might thank God for the way in which He has led us for the past 
fifty years, and to look forward to the years that are to come, and 
see something of the work opening before us. I hope we may not 
be liited up with pride as we think of all that God has enabled us 
to do in this city, and throughout this land, and perhaps even 
beyond the borders of Canada. When we think of it all we are 
rather humbled, and would give all the glory to Him who has given 
us this great opportunity of service for young men. 

“There are upon this platform a few .of the men who have seen 
all the years that this Association has seen. We are honoured in 
their presence to-night, and it is with reverence that we welcome 
them, and we envy them the feelings they must have as they sit 
here and see what God has wrought, and what He has permitted to 
grow from that seed they planted fifty years ago. We have here 
also our city pastors. We can say in Montreal that the city pastors 
look upon the Association, not as a rival, but as a hand of the 
Church put out to take hold of this work which the church must do. 
We have here our Provincial Committee, a committee with whom it 
is a pleasure to work, and with whom we have been blessed in 
working all these years. We have here also the International Com- 
mittee. What shall I say about them? The fact is, the work be- 
tween this Association and the International Committee has been 
such, and always will be such, that they are just a part of the 
family, and are not even visitors here to-night. We look upon 
them as brothers who have come home. But there are with us 
to-night others who have come across the sea, and yet are loyal to 
the same flag that waves over us here. We are glad to welcome 
these brethren from the old land that have journeyed so far to see 
how the child of the Mother Country has gotten on in these fifty 
years. 

“ But beyond the bounds even of the British Empire, which we are 
so proud to think extends so far, we are honoured by the presence 
of those from other parts of the world—for this is now a world wide 
brotherhood, and whenever one member rejoices, all the members 
throughout the world-rejoice. ; 

“And then our younger brother is up here. Boston, who came 
so near being our twin, and yet whom we are so proud to feel is just 


47 


a little younger than we are—Boston has come here to see if the 
elder brother has departed from the faith once delivered to the 
saints. And London is here, the home of the parent association, 
and we are proud that we are honoured with a visit from the mother 
association of the world. London comes over to do honour to this 
child that was born fifty years ago. But there is yet higher 
honour for us to-night, for, sitting on the right of the line is the son 
of the honoured founder of the Association. I am glad I am a 
Williams. We are proud to-night that Mr. Howard Williams has 
come here as a representative of his father, and is to unveil for us 
on Monday the tablet that commemorates fiity years of association 
work. .Then again on the other end of the line is the son of 
the chairman of the first meeting when this association was formed, 
Mr. Alfred E. Marling, from New York City,—two honoured sons 
of two honoured fathers. 

“We welcome you all here to-night. While I am here as Presi- 
dent of the Association to present not only my own welcome, but 
that of the Board of Directors, there is another welcome that is not 
heard in this hall, and yet it is deeper than any other that can 
be given, and it comes to you from the thousands of young men 
who have come in contact with this Association, and through that 
contact have had their lives led to higher and better things. We are 
proud to think that in all these years hundreds and thousands of 
men have had their lives lifted up from selfishness and sin to the 
praise of God, who created them, and it is their gratitude and wel- 
come that is extended to-night as we are gathered here.” 


Mr. D. A. Bunce, the General Secretary, then presented 
the Historical Sketch of the Association, which had been 
prepared, reading extracts and making comments thereon. 
As this sketch has been published copies may be obtained at 
the Association. After singing the hymn, * Oh, for a thou- 
sand tongues to sing,” greetings were received as follows :— 


Greetings from the Ministerial Association. 


Rev. James Fleck, on behalf of the Ministerial Association, 
presented the following resolution, adopted by the Ministerial 
Association of the city of Montreal, at the meeting held on 
Thursday, 6th June :— 


“ Whereas, some three thousand delegates, including prominent 
Christian workers from all parts of the world, are gathering for 
the celebration, in the City of Boston, of the Fiftieth Anniversary of 
the inception of Young Men’s Christian Associations on chis conti- 
nent, and 

“Whereas, Montreal has the honour of being the first city in 
which this organization for the saving and developing of young iren 
was formed, and 

“Whereas, a preliminary celebration of this Jubilee is to be held 
in this city from the eighth to the tenth of June, be it hereby 

“Resolved, That the Protestant Ministers of Montreal, in special 


48 


meeting assembled, record their gratitude to God for the birth of 
this beneficent agency, for its enormous growth during the half 
century of its existence, and for the great service it has rendered in 
the making of Christian men, and’ it is further 

“ Resolved, That we recognize in the Association not a rival sect, 
nor a substitute for the Church of Christ, but an institute that supple- 
ments the work of all the churches in providing Christian companion- 
ship for our young men, with admirable facilities for their physical, 
mental, and spiritual improvement. 

“We commend the Association to the blessinz of God, to the 
generous support of all good people, and to the confidence of our 
young men, 

“On behalf of the Ministerial Association of Montreal.” 

“James Fleck.” 


Greetings from the International Committee. 


Dr. Lucren C. WARNER, of New York, Chairman of the 
International Committee, said :— 

“Tt gives me great pleasure to 
bring to the Montreal Association 
the greetings of the International 
Committee. I feel conscious of that 
fellowship which has been mention- 
ed by the President, and I have 
such a homelike feeling in Mont- 
real that I hardly knew whether 
those present are Americans and I 
am a Canadian, or whether they are 
Canadians and I am a Yankee. On 
looking back over the fifty years of 
the Association’s life in this coun- 
try, I can only say—What has 
God wrought. Fifty years ago 
our country was just entering upon 
the most marked material prosper- 
ity that had ever blessed any land 
in the world. Our vacant land was 
being filled up, our hamlets changed 
to villages, our villages to cities 
and our cities to great metropolitan 
cities, and wifh these changes and developments came new tempta- 
tions to the young men and new trials to the Church. But it was 
divinely appointed that at this point there should be developed the 
Young Men’s Christian Association, to get hold of these young men 
in our cities and hold them for Christ and for the Church. And 
the work has developed all along the line. Its educational system, 
its college branches and railroad branches, fill a want that nothing 
else could fill, and in this development Canada and the United States 
have worked together. 

“It is a source of great pleasure and gratification to us that we 
have as the vice-chairman of the International Committee, the son 
of the man who presided at the first meeting in Montreal for the 
establishment of the work on this continent. 


49 
Greetings from the Provincial Committee. 


Mr. Joun PENMAN, of Paris, Ont., Chairman of the Provin- 
cial Committee, said :— 


“TY have come to bring the greetings from the Associations 
throughout the Dominion, stretching from Cape Breton on the 
Atlantic coast to Vancouver on the Pacific, and to join in thanks 
and praise to God for the past. We are astonished when we look 
around and see the advancement the Association movement has 
made in the last fifty years, particularly the latter half of that period. 
When the Association was started and the earlier ones formed, it 
was simply a banding together of young men for Christian service. 
But to-day it is astonishing to see the all-round work for the body, for 
the mind, and for the spirit which was being done. Then there is 
the railway branch, the college branch, and the military camps. All 
these are the results of the work of the brave men who had had 
the courage to found the Association fifty years ago. Then there 
was the work for boys, and this was one of the most important 
works in the future. In the past it had only been possible to reach 
the larger cities, but the Associations to-day were stretching out 
their hands to help those in smaller places, and organizations were 
springing up in towns and villages which would produce great re- 
sults in the future. May God's richest blessing rest on the Montreal 
Association, and all other Associations, and may the secretaries and 
members take as their motto—* Whatever thy hand findeth to do, do 
it with thy might.” 


Mr. ALFRED E. Martine, of New York city :— 


“T do not know whether I should speak as a New Yorker, or as 
a son of my father, or a Canadian. born in Toronto. But which- 
ever one of the three, I am very glad to be in Montreal, and wish 
my father could have been here as well. I feel sure that my father 
and those who have gone before, would look down in congratulation 
and satisfaction upon the work which they had started fifty years 
ago, and which had continued so magnificently up to the present 
moment. 

“In these Jubilee proceedings we should not dwell too much on 
the past, marvellous as it had been. We cannot live on our past, 
and the present is but the stepping stone to the future. President 
Styker, of Hamilton College, says of the man who speaks constantly 
of his ancestors that you can be well assured the best of him is 
underground. I pray for God’s richest blessing upon the future of 
this great work, and hope we may all be worthy of the heritage 
which has been bequeathed to us.” 


50 
Greetings from the English Nationa! Council. 


Mr. W. H. Mitts, of London, England, Secretary of the 
English National Council, said :— 

“T would like to say in one brief 
word as to how deep has been 
the thankfulness with which we 
had heard from time to time of 
the progress of the work of the 
Association in Montreal and 
throughout Canada, and it is 
this good work which has 
brought so large a number of 
delegates from across the At- 
lantic to see it. After hearing 
the excellent report presented 
by Mr. Budge, all I can say 
would be summed up in four 
words, ‘Well done, go on.’ 
Lord Kinnaird will present the 
congratulations of the National 
Council, with an address for 
your acceptance.” 


Lorp Kinnatrp, of London, England, said :— 


“An honour has been given 
me as one of the Vice-Presi- 
dents of the National Council, 
in asking me to hand over an 
address to the Montreal Asso- 
ciation. It has required great 
force of will to keep Sir George 
Williams, our honoured and 
revered President, from  dis- 
obeying any order that any | 
friend or any doctor could give 
him. The address which I have 
been asked to present contains 
amongst its signers many well- 
known names, and one is very 
well-known and very much loved 
in Canada and many parts of 
the world; I refer to Lord 
Aberdeen, who, with his good 
wife, has done so much good 
and are so well known in 
Christian work. 

“We have a great deal to thank God for, but the work of the 
Association is only beginning. It seems to be growing greater 
all the time, and the more work done, the more there seems to be 
done. To-day there are three hundred millions of our fellow subjects 
who are waiting for the message to be sent to them in India, and 
it is our duty to heed the call. 


dl 


“The Associations on the other side have learned many lessons 
from those on this side, and they are learning lessons on_ this 
occasion. I am glad of the opportunity of seeing what a building 
should be for the benefit of young men. We will go back having 
seen what Christian liberality can do, and I hope we shall profit by 
the lesson.” 

The address was then presented and received on behalf of the 
Asscciation by Mr. John Penman, Chairman of the Provincial 
Committee. 


ADDRESS OF ENGLISH NATIONAL COUNCIL, 


The President, Vice-Presidents, and Council of the English 
National Union, to the Delegates and Representatives of the 
Young Men’s Christian Associations of the Dominion of 


Canada, Montreal, 1901. 
“Esteemed and Dear Brethren,— 

“The occasion of your assem- 
bling to commemorate the Jubilee 
of the Founding of the Montreal 
Young Men’s Christian Association 
presents an opportunity, of which 
we gladly avail ourselves, to convey 
to you, and, through you, to the 
entire membership of your Associa- 
tions, the heartiest greetings of As- 
sociations in the Mother Country. 
We unite with the other organized 
unions of Associations throughout 
the Empire, in congratulating you 
upon the good work accomplished 
during the past fifty years in all the 
more populous centres of the Do- 
minion; while we recognize with 
deep thankfulness the rich and mani- 
fold blessings which God has graci- 
ously bestowed upon your labors. 

“Fathers and mothers in the Home Land greatly appreciate your 
loving care for their sons, who in such large numbers come to reside 
in your country, and who, but for the cordial welcome extended to 
them by your Associations, would be exposed to grave peril and 
temptation. 

“ Formed upon the best models, your Associations have derived 
invaluable stimulus and support from their incorporation in the 
North American Federation; and we esteem it highly advantageous 
to the Home Associations, also, to be thereby brought into more 
intimate contact with the work for young men carried on with such 
conspicuous success throughout your entire Continent. 

“Increased facilities of communication, and the augrientation of 
business relations between different portions of the Enipire, have 
tended to knit more closely the ties of kindred and nationality; and 
our Home Associations count it a great privilege io be able row, 


52 


under the auspices of the British and Colonial Union, to welcome 
Delegates from the Associations of the Dominion, as well as from 
those of other Colonies and Dependencies, at the annual British 
Conferences, as well as at meetings of their Representative Councils. 
The World Tour of Mr. and Mrs. Oatts, undertaken at the instance 
of the English Council in the interests of Colonial work, expresses 
the great value we attach to the opportunities thus afforded for pro- 
moting fuller intercourse with your Associations, and thereby 
strengthening the bonds of sympathy and mutual interest which link 
the whole of the Associations together in a common aim and service. 

“We greatly rejoice in the signal honour already placed upon your 
labours, and pray that, in the new era upon which you are entering, 
God will give you to experience in even richer abundance the tokens 
of His favour and goodness—that He will “multiply your seed sown, 
increase the fruits of your righteousness,” and “‘stablish you in every 
good word and work.” 


Signed on behalf of the Council, 
GEORGE WILLIAMS, Kt., President.

Greetings from the World’s Committee. 


Mr. Cuar_tes Fermaup, of Geneva, Switzerland, General 
Secretary of the World’s Committee, said -— 


“In the twenty-two years 
since I have visited Montreal, 
great developments have taken 
place in the Young Men’s Chris- 
tian Association. I bring you 
the greetings of the Worl1's 
Committee, and the wish they 
send to the Montreal Associa- 
tion, and the Associations 
throughout the Dominion of 
Canada is that ‘they should 
be separated men of might, men 
fit for the battle, and for the 
King, men whose faces were 
like the faces of lions,’ or as 
our translation says, ‘whose 
courage was like the courage of 
lions, and as swift as the roe on 
the mountains. When I say I 
bring you the greetings of the 
World’s Committee, I mean the 
greetings of the Associations all 
over the world, and not only of the committee at Geneva. All over 
the world the eyes of the Young Men’s Christian Associations are 
centred on this Jubilee celebration. What is wanted in Association 
work to-day is young men who know Christ for their Saviour, and 
knowing him well, will go out to the people with a great courage, 
men who are ready to obey and go wherever they are needed. The 
work in Montreal must be in good hands, or it would not have 
prospered and been blessed the way it has.” 


Greetings from Boston. 


Mr. GeorGeE A. MIner, of Boston, said :-— 


“T have come with a heart full of greetings from the Boston 
Association, the twin brother as it had been called, and I have 
brought their warmest greetings to the Montreal Association on the 
occasion of your Jubilee Celebration. I do this with greater pleasure 
because I am a Canadian. I feel that I am both a pretty good 
Canadian and a good American, but there is one thing I am more 
proud of, and that is to have been a charter member of the Boston 
Young Men’s Christian Association. For four years I was President, 
and during that period the beautiful building in which we are at 
present was erected. I have been delegated by the friends in Bos- 
ton to give a hearty invitation to all to come to their homes and 
hearts during the next week, and I know that those who are coming 
to the Jubilee Celebration of the Associations will receiye great 
benefit.” 


Greetings from the 
Parent Association, 


At this point the Chair- 
man introduced Mr. J. H. Put- 
terill, Secretary of the Central 
Young Men’s Christian Asso- 
ciation of London, England, 
who read an illuminated ad- 
dress prepared by the parent 
Association, the text of which 


appears on opposite page. 


Mr. Howarp WIttiams, son of Sir George -Williams, in 
making the presentation made the following remarks :— 


“Mr. Chairman, in asking : 
you to accept for the Association 
this expression of our congratula- 
tions and good wishes, may I re- 
quest you to allow this to be hung 
up in one of your beautiful rooms, 
so that it may be a memorial to all 
time of the good feeling existing 
detween the oldest Associations in 
the Old World and in the New. 
We inthe Old Country have much 
to thank you for and I am glad 
of this opportunity of expressing 
our appreciation of the way you 
have looked after our boys when 
they have come across the ocean. 
Many a father in the Old Country 
has thanked God for this Associa- 
tion when his boy was coming to 
Canada, and many a mother has 
had her tears dried when she has been saying good-bye to her boy, 
and her tears turned to smiles when she remembered that letter in 
his pocket to Mr. Budge. We have come across the Atlantic to 
join you in celebrating this Jubilee. We come as_ brothers to 
brothers, with our hearts full of love and thankfulness for what has 
been done, and we believe in looking in your faces and shaking 
hands with the members of the Association, as we shall during the 
next two or three days, we shall increase our zeal for the work, and 
go home with a fresh inspiration to do better service than in the ® 
past in our own Associations.”
