Montreal’s Reply to these Greetings, 


Mr. H. B. Ames, on behalf of the Montreal Association, 
replied to the greetings :— 


“Mr. Chairman: I think you will all admit that upon my shoul- 
ders has fallen the most difficult task of the evening. I am not to 
address the audience, I am to address the platform, and I am to 
endeavour in some way to express the appreciation that the Montreal 
Association feels at the presence of these friends of ours with u: 
to-night, and with the words of cordial greeting that have fallen from 
their lips. 


“We have, I think, before us to-night, an opportunity which will 
probably never be equalled in the lives of any of us, although the 
majority of those in this room are yet young men. We have the 
opportunity to see, and to listen to men whose names are deeply 
graven in the history of the Young Men’s Christian Association. 
Never, do I believe, shall we have an opportunity of seeing upon a 
platiorm in the city of Montreal men who represent every epoch of 
Association history, as do those who are with us to-night. We are 
justly proud of ourselves because we realize that the seven thousand 
Associations scattered throughout the world, and nearly half a 
million members scattered throughout the globe all have their eyes 
turned to the Montreal Association. We realize, that for this night 
at least, we are the centre of the Association universe, and it is 
indeed grateful that we are, when from our own city and from each 
concentric ring about our city on and on to the furthest limits of the 
world, come these words of greeting, congratulation, sympathy and 
good cheer. 


“ First, it is very gratifying that we should be appreciated here in 
our own city by those men who are undoubtedly the best cipable of 
judging the value of Christian service, namely, our own Christian 
pastors. That these gentlemen should have gathered in special as- - 
sembly, and should have passed resolutions so kindly minded, and 
should have deputed one whom we so highly respect to come and 
present this resolution, causes us feelings of the deepest joy, and I 
assure Mr. Fleck we will treasure in the archives of the Association 
for many years the document he has been kind enough to deposit 
with us. 


* And again, for all of us who are Canadians, and it looks to-night 
as though nearly all good men were Canadians,—but all of us who 
are Canadians were glad to hear the words of cheer that came to us 
from the honoured Chairman of the Provincial Committee. We have 
a realizing sense that so long as men of that stamp and that sound 
judgment, and breadth of idea, and Christian fortitude, which Mr. 
Penman has, are in control of our provincial work, we shall ever 
advance abreast of the times. 


“And then, too, from our twin brother, over whom, you know, we 
have always claimed a slight advantage, in point of antiquity, and over 
whom we occasionally press that advantage, from the friends in 
Boston we too are glad to hear such welcome words. We are glad 


57 


they should come here to assist in this celebration. We will 
endeavour to go in large numbers to assist them in their subsequent 
celebration. 


“Tt is pleasant to feel, too, that we are part of a great whole, and 
that this boundary line which has been referred to by Dr. Warner 
to-night, which he expresses the wish may some day be abolished, 
which wish we perhaps are not quite so willing to admit—it is 
gratifying to feel that we are part of one great whole, and this imagin- 
ary line which separates us does not separate us in Christian hopes 
and aspirations. And I think we cannot be too grateful for what 
the International Committee is doing for this, and for the other 
Canadian Associations. Think what it means to have the Interna- 
tional Committee to fall back on for guidance and help, and counsel, 
and we appreciate it highly that their representative should be here 
to-night to extend to us the right hand of fellowship. 


“And still the circle broadens and we cross the ocean, and our 
thoughts rest upon the old land. We think of the old city wherein 
was founded this Association, and turn our eyes to the picture of the 
founder facing us, enveloped in the flags of several nations. We feel 
that to have upon our platform to-night those who represent the 
names of Williams and Marling, two names which stand for first 
principles, both in the London and Montreal Association, is a great 
honour, and we will indeed cherish this beautiful illuminated address 
that has been given us. This resolution shall be hung where it may 
be seen in our Association, where those of us who are here to-night 
may grow familiar with its spirit and thought, and where those of us 
as we grow older and learn to love it, shall pass it on to those who 
come after us, and tell them to cherish it as long as the Association 
stands in Montreal. 


“And then the International representative from Geneva comes 
to us with warm heart and kind words, and assures us that we are 
remembered also on the Continent of Europe, that we form a part 
of a still larger circle, that we.are doing similar work and have similar 
aspirations, and similar ideals with these young men who speak many 
languages in Continental Europe. It is to us who are in the thick 
of the fight, to us who are still young men, an inspiration and help 
to know that we form part of one great institution serving one 
common Master, ever ready to lend a helping hand the one to the 
other, ever lifting up our hearts in prayer to one common God. 


“In conclusion let me thank you one and all on behalf of this 
gathering, on behalf of those whom they represent, our two thousand 
and odd members, on behalf of all the Association members of the 
Dominion of Canada, who unite in spirit with us to-night, let me 
thank you for your presence and for the words of friendly greeting 
you have extended to us.” 


The meeting closed with the hymn, “ Ye servants of God 
your Master proclaim.” 


58 


On Sunday morning at 9.30 the visit- 
ing delegates and members of the Associa- 
tion met in Association Hall for a praise 
and thanksgiving meeting at which Mr. 
Ricuarp C. Morse, General Secretary of 
the International Committee presided. 

At the same hour a meeting for boys 
was held in the lower lecture hall by the 
Junior Executive Committee at which 
addresses were delivered by Mr. Howard 
Williams, of London, England, Mr. C. 
B. Willis, of Milwaukee, and Mr. Chas. 
Fermaud, of Geneva, Switzerland. 

On Sunday afternoon at 3.45 o’clock a public meeting was 
held in St. James Methodist Church, at which Mr. C. T. 
Williams, President of the Association, was in the chair. The 
large edifice was filled with a thoroughly representative audi- 
ence. The meeting opened with * All hail the power of 
Jesus’ name,” after which the Rev. G. Osborne Troop led in 
prayer, and the Rey. Dr. McWilliams read the Scriptures. 
Addresses were then delivered as follows :— 


Lorp KINNAIRD said :— 


“T have been asked to attend, not as an orator, but as a plain 
business man, to bring the most hearty congratulations and good 
wishes from the other side. We meet at a memorable time in our 
Empire’s history, because we have lost one under whose flag and 
under whose revered name we have labored, and whose work and 
life we all admired, and who had shown her appreciation of the work 
of the Young Men’s Christian Association on the occasion of the 
Jubilee some years ago, when all the delegates were invited to Wind- 
sor Castle and were treated right royally. Times were also important 
in our Empire’s history during the last eighteen months, and I have 
found the same sentiment here in regard to the war as was to be 
found at home, and many a young life had been laid down in the 
service of the Empire, not only from the Mother Land, but also from 
Canada and all our other colonies. 

“ During the last fifty years great changes have taken place, and 
from the history of the Association in Montreal which had been given 
by Mr. Budge, one could see the changes that had taken place here 
during that time. Sir George Williams himself fifty years ago could 
never have thought of the world-wide influence of the Associations of 
to-day, though he had more faith than most men, and to-day the 
motto which Sir George Williams and his associates took to them- 
selves was still being carried out ‘Young men for Jesus Christ, and 
Christ for young men.’ ” 

“The work of to-day could only be successfully carried on by a 
consecrated membership, a consecrated committee force, a cohsecrat- 
ed secretary, and all these essentials would have to work together 
in order that the work might be successfully done. But even when 


59 


our local work was well done our duty was not wholly accomplished, 
for greater work lay still before us. In India there were three 
hundred millions of young men waiting to receive the gospel, whilst 
here we had only half a million, and as half a million was to three 
hundred millions so our responsibilities were greater in non-Christian 
India. We have lately seen what the British Empire can do if a 
certain part of it is in danger. From every quarter of the globe help 
came, and that quickly, and now, when the call was being made for 
help in Christ’s kingdom, help should come just as quickly. <A 
British army officer had been asked how long it would take the 
British Army to take the Queen’s proclamation all over the world, 
and he had worked out what two hundred thousand men could do, 
and he said he would undertake to do the work in from 15 to 18 
months. The Church has for the last twenty centuries been trying 
to take Christ’s proclamation around the world, and has not finished 
its work yet. It was time we were up and doing, realizing the 
responsibility God has placed upon us. I trust all present will join 
in the work of winning the young men of this world for Jesus Christ.” 


Mr. W. M. Oarts, of Glasgow, said :— 


“One is too likely to 
take it for granted in such 
an audience that everyone 
present knows all about the 
work of the Young Men’s 
Christian Association, but I 
am going to appeal to them 
on its behalf, and hope my 
appeal will not be in vain. 
Fifty-seven years ago in 
George Williams’ office in 
London, 13 young men 
githered together and start- 
ed the London Young 
Men’s Christian Associa- 
tion, and from that small 
beginning there has spread 
this world-wide organiza- 
tion, with over seven thou- 
sand. I have been travel- 
ling some eighteen months 
and have gone 42,000 miles, all the time within sight of the British 
flag, and I have seen much during this journey of the work of the 
Young Men’s Christian Association. I have seen the Association 
away up in the snows of Lapland, away down in the Sunny South of 
Italy. I have visited the Association in Cairo where 27 young men 
are gathered together to worship God, and have fellowship and 
communion together. I have gone up to the Holy City, and as I 
passed through the Jaffa Gate met the well-known letters Y. M; C. A. 
in the city of the Great King. Then we went to the city of Nazareth 
where Christ was born, and we were helpful in establishing a Young 
Men’s Christian Association there, and Mrs. Oatts had assisted to 
establish a branch of the Youfig Women’s Christian Association, and 
so the good work was going on, and spreading. The work the Young 
Men’s Christian Associations was doing could be well illustrated by 


. 


60 


giving an instance which came to my knowledge. A young man left 
Glasgow for Montreal, and took with him a letter of introduction to 
Mr. Budge. He was given a hearty welcome, and was introduced to 
and became friends with the Christian young men there, and work was 
found for him. He had not been a month in Montreal before he 
sickened, and was taken to the hospital. The only ones coming to 
see him during the hours of his sickness were the members of the 
Young Men’s Christian Association. There he lay, three thousand 
miles away from home, and there he lingered and died. Did the 
Association leave him even then? No, they brought the remains of 
that young man down to their rooms, had a religious service over his 
remains, and followed his body to its last resting place. What a 
solace this was to his friends on the other side, to know he had not 
died friendless and alone. This was the work of the Young Men’s 
Christian Association, and what was being done all over the world. 

“Tn most worldly affairs one could see immense enthusiasm 
displayed. In Scotland I have seen a great many football matches, 
some of them attended by as many as 70,000 people, and what enthu- 
siasm was created. In New York Mr. Morse had taken me to see 
a baseball game. There had been some twenty of thirty thousand 
people there, and what enthusiasm there was. How every good play 
was cheered to the echo. There was plenty of enthusiasm for the 
things of this world, and we want that enthusiasm won over to the 
side of Christ. Christ Himself had that enthusiasm, or He could 
never have set his face to go up to Jerusalem that He might suffer 
and die for a lost world. Think of the enthusiasm of the Apostle 
Paul, “‘ This one thing I do,” and we want the young men of to-day 
not to have one whit less enthusiasm, but_to bring that enthusiasm 
and lay it upon the altar for the service to Jesus Christ. 

“Young manhood is a time of fierce temptation and is a great 
crisis in the lives of all young men. The open door of the Young 
Men’s Christian Association, the warm and loving grasp of the 
Secretary of the Association, was a thing to help a young man in 
that crisis, and I call upon those present to help on this work in the 
name of our risen Saviour.” 


THE ACHIEVEMENTS AND POSSIBILITIES OF THE 
ASSOCIATION MOVEMENT OF NORTH AMERICA. 


Mr. Joun R. Mort, of New York :— 


“Your President has introduced me 
as the prophet of the Young Men’s 
Christian Association, but before begin- 
ning to prophesy let me dwell a little 
on history. 

“The achievements of the Young 
Men’s Christian Association of North 
America have been of such extent, 
power, and significance, as to convince 
even the skeptical that Almighty God 
is in this work. The fact that the 
number of Associations of young men 
banded together in the name of our 
risen Lord, has increased from two in 
1851 to fifteen hundred at the present 

“time, is in itself an achievement which 


61 


should arrest attention. The fact that in those days there were less 
than one hundred young men banded together for the specific 
purpose of reaching their fellows, whereas to-day we have the vast 
army of 255,000 young men in these two sister countries alone, who 
have associated their efforts for the extension of God’s kingdom 
among young men, also demonstrates the reality of the work of God 
among young men of our time. Even as recently as 1869 there was 
only one building on the entire continent devoted to this work, 
whereas to-day we have not far from four hundred of these buildings, 
worth over twenty-five millions of dollars; and this fact has led many 
a man to enquire into the causes of the development of this movement 
and to pledge to it his allegiance. 

“The fact that during the last fifty years a new calling or profes- 
sion has been created, in the ranks of which to-day we find not less 
than fifteen hundred young men —a _ profession possessing such 
possibilities that it presents powerful claims to the strongest young 
men of the colleges and universities of our day, has been in turn the 
means of convincing many that here is a great work to do, and that 
it is being increasingly well done. 

“TI do not pause to enlarge upon such facts because that simply 
calls attention to means. It signifies not so much that there are a 
quarter of a million young men banded together in North America 
for this purpose, that we have over twenty-five millions worth of 
property, that there are fifteen hundred trained leaders. These are 
simply means to large ends, and before God, who calls us to give 
an account of the use of our talents, we have the right to expect that 
the use of these means would lead to large and convincing achieye- 
ments, and we have not been disappointed in our expectation. 

‘Notice in rapid summary some of the great achievements which 
have been wrought within the half century, as a result of this inspired 
movement. In the first place, the Young Men’s Christian Associa- 
tion has been the first great movement of laymen in the Christian 
Church. It has inaugurated, stimulated, and led the varied lay forces, 
which are to-day so prominent, and increasing in the different 
branches of the all-embracing Church of Jesus Christ. This 
movement was founded by a layman—God bless him richly to-day— 
it has been developed by laymen, and its distinguishing characteristic 
is that it is a lay movement. It should be emphasized, however, 
that it is working in harmony with and under the valuable suggestion 
of the clerical leaders of all sections of the Church of God. 

“This movement has placed before the world, and done much to 
realize the true ideal of young manhood—a symmetrical young 
manhood, a Christ-like young manhood. It seeks so to develop the 
body that it will endure the strain of this intense age of competition. 
Moreover, it emphasises the importance of the mind receiving the 
higher furnishing and finishing, the enriching and calling out of the 
social nature, and the salvation of the soul—the sending of the young 
man into the world to stand four-square to every wind that blows. 

“We notice, in reviewing the past fifty years, that the Young 
Men’s Christian Association has developed such an organization and 
agencies as have enabled it in a great measure to become all things 
unto all classes of young men. It has applied with splendid results 
this scriptural principle. It has involved the setting of a class of 
young men to work for the young men of that particular class; as, 


62 


for instance, in the college work, in the railroad work, the army work, 
the naval work, and the work among all the varied classes of our 
continent. 

The Young Men’s Christian Association in these fifty years has 
done much to break down barriers between man and man, and to fuse 
together the different classes in society. Take the railroad work, 
for example. What other organization to-day is bringing together 
the railroad manager and the lowest employee on a common platform, 
leading them to understand the point of view of one another, and to 
appreciate the spirit of one another, and to work for common ends? 
Take the College Associations. Not long since I visited a college on 
this continent where the son of one of the richest men on this side of 
the Atlantic was a student. I found that young man working on the 
sane committee with other young men who were earning their way 
through college by waiting on tables. These men worked together 
with perfect understanding and sympathy, and they will continue to 
appreciate each other, and as a result, will help to work out a larger 
and more successful solution of the social problems of our day. 

“The Association movement of North America has carried 
forward on behalf of young men an evangelistic campaign of such 
mighty sweep and power that an increasing number of young men 
have been ushered into the kingdom of our Lord and Saviour Jesus 
Christ. This is what the movement was called into being for, and 
when it ceases to stand for this, let it disband. It was the impulse 
inspired of God in the mind of our honoured founder. It has been 
the crowning glory of the Young Men’s Christian Association. The 
imagination staggers to-day as it tries to grasp the vast number of 
young men whose robes have been washed in the blood of the Lamb 
as a result of the beneficent work of these societies. 

“The Associations have afforded a striking demonstration of the 
reality of the great spiritual forces of the world, and this has been a 
service of great significance in an age, and on a continent in which 
the forces of materialism are so. strong, and where they are so increas- 
ing. I refer to such great spiritual realities as the living Christ, not 
one dead away back there centuries ago, but one living, and saving, 
and transforming the lives of tempted and doubting young men of 
to-day; the dynamic and quickening influence of the Word of God; 
the mountain-removing power of prayer, and the transforming 
influence of the Spirit of God working through organization and 
consecrated personal effort. These great forces have been made more 
real and commanding and felt, as a result of the work of these 
societies. 

“While the Associations have been doing the regular work for 
which they were called into being, they have, both directly and 
indirectly, by example given rise to other great spiritual movements. 
I need only give their names. Reasons could be given why each one of 
these is included were it necessary. Note the list : The Evangelical 
Alliance; the Young Women’s Christian Association ; the Young 
People’s Society of Christian Endeavour, which in turn did so much 
to suggest the great denominational movements, and in all of these 
we find some six millions of young people in these two countries 
alone; the Inter-Seminary Missionary Alliance of Students; the 


Student Volunteer Movement for Foreign Missions; the World’s 


Student Christian Federation. I might speak also of the evangelistic 


63 


movement of the last generation led by Mr. Moody, who gave testi- 
mony that the Young Men’s Christian Association had given him this 
impulse and much of his training. The mere catalogue of these great 
movements is impressive. 

“The mill-streams that move the great machinery of the world 
rise in solitary places. And when we see such vast, varied and benefi- 
cent activities we believe that away back there somewhere in the 
secret place a consecrated heart opened, Almighty God spoke His 
message and it was heard and obeyed. 

“The Young Men’s Christian Association movement of North 
America, in league with our brothers of the British Isles, have trans- 
planted the Association idea to the great non-Christian countries of 
the world. We have gone out there, and there was abundant need 
of our going. Our object has been to make the universities and the 
city communities strongholds and propagating centres of pure and 
aggressive Christianity. In response to the call of the missionaries 
of the non-Christian countries, to place at their disposal this agency 
so useful at home, there where it is so much more needed. There 
comes back to memory to-day the awful need of the young men of 
the unevangelized world as I have had opportunity to see it. At 
times it comes back to haunt me in the watches of the night. If my 
life be spared, I hope a few months hence to put my life once more 
alongside the fiercely-tempted young men of India, of China and of 
Japan, to help them in their battles. 

“ Another service, which I simply touch, although very significant, 
is that the Young Men’s Christian Associations have done much to 
emphasize and to realize true Christian unity. They have afforded a 
splendid demonstration of the fact that there is one body and one 
spirit, even as ye were also called in one hope of your calling, one 
Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and father of all who is over 
all, and through all, and in all. Only as we put our lives by the life 
of Christ when He offered the prayer that we all might be one, do we 
begin to realize what this service means. 

“And now let me call attention to some regions beyond, and as 
I do so let us ask ourselves the question: If this movement with such 
small and humble beginnings, has resulted in such wonderful achieve- 
ments, what may we not expect from God during the next fifty years? 

“T would say the first region beyond is the development of this 
work on the lines which have already been projected. We have only 
touched the fringe of the possibilities of this movement in any one 
department. It matters not what department you take. Do you 
take railroad work? Should we be satisfied with touching only forty- 
five thousand out of one million railroad men in the United States 
and Canada ? Talk about students: Should we be satisfied with 
having gathered within our fold only thirty-five thousand students 
and professors of these countries out of over two hundred thousand? 
And so on through the different classes and the different phases of 
this work. You and I are going to live to see the day when in the 
educational classes of the Young Men’s Christian Associations there 
will be more young men than we have in the colleges of our conti- 
nent to-day. We are going to live to see the day when in every city 
of considerable importance, and in the smaller towns there will be 
facilities for the development of the body. We are going to live to 
see the day when the spiritual achievements of this work are going to 
put to shame the achievements which are behind us. 


64 


“A second region beyond is in the realm of extending the Associa- 
tion. We talk about University Extension to-day, and by that we 
mean taking the university to people who cannot go to the university. 
The development of the next fifty years is going to be, not so much 
what takes place in the Association building as what goes out from 
the Association building. We are going to take the Young Men’s 
Christian Association where the young men are. We are already 
beginning to do this in the factories, on the naval vessels, and in 
other places where young men are doing their work, and spending 
their leisure time. We are also going to emphasize organized and 
delegated personal work for making Christ known and felt where the 
young men are having their sports, and doing their work. In so doing 
we shall be imitating Christ. 

“ A third region beyond will be suggested by the expansion of the 
population of these two countries. I am within bounds when I 
predict to-day that within fifty years the population of the United 
States and Canada will more than double, and the larger extension is 
going to be in this Dominion, and for obvious reasons. The Young 
Men’s Christian Associations of the next fifty years must grapple, 
therefore, not only with fifteen million young men of to-day, but 
they must get ready to deal with thirty millions. And more than 
the welfare of thirty million young men is involved, because on this 
continent, providentially situated between the two great oceans, in this 
age of world-wide expansion, these two countries, together with the 
British Isles, are going to be looked upon increasingly as a great 
pare of operations for the world-wide extension of the kingdom of 

rist. 

“Another region beyond are the fifteen million boys of North 
America, whose number within a half-century will increase to thirty 
millions. The statesmen of our movement, and the leaders of it must 
begin to get ready for grappling with this great problem. It is never 
too soon to prepare to do a great work. And, by the way, this work 
for boys is the most hopeful and fruitful work before us. Why ? 
You save a young man and you are dealing with addition, but when 
you save a boy you deal with multiplication. 

“There is a region beyond upon which I do not trust myself to 
enlarge, and that is the innumerable multitude of young men of less 
favored lands in the non-Christian world. How many are there? 
Now less than two hundred millions of them. In Canada and the 
United States we have one secretary for every ten thousand young 
men; in those non-Christian nations we have only one to every ten 
millions. Is this a fair distribution? If Christ were here to-day to 
pass in judgment upon the distribution of the light bearers and the 
Christian leaders, would He be satisfied? Judging by His command, 
by His teachings, and by His example, He would call for a more 
wide-spread diffusion of the leaders of our work among the non-Chris- 
tian nations. This is the greatest work that has been given to the 
Young Men’s Christian Association of North America, and for other 
Protestant countries to do. To my brethren of the British Isles I 
do not need to appeal, nor to our brethren from Germany, Scandi- 
navia and other places. We understand each other, and hand in 
hand we are going to go forward in this movement and plant the 
Young Men’s Christian Association in every great metropolitan and 
student centre in the non-Christian world. 


65 


“The sixth region beyond is in the realm of a more aggressive 
wariare against the forces of evil. When I consider to-day the 
magnitude of the forces of evil on this continent, as I am obliged to 
see them, when I recognize the ingenuity and the enterprise of the 
leaders of these forces of evil, when I notice, with faint heart at times, 
the vindictiveness and the awiul cruelty of these forces of evil, I am 
led to believe that Christ would have us be inspired with more of that 
enthusiasm of which we have heard so eloquently from our brother 
from Scotland, (Mr. Oatts), this afternoon. Yes, more of that 
enthusiasm. Not long since I went back to my own 
town in the West, where I spent the larger part of my life, 
and I saw strong men take away a young man with whom I 
used to go to school before I went to college. They took him away 
to the asylum of mental deaths. Sin did it. I will fight it until I 
die. Why should we not fight it? Everything which has caused 
suffering and loss and sorrow, and shame, and death, is traceable to 
sin. I appeal therefore to the young men of Montreal and of the 
other Associations here represented, that we declare uncompromising 
and aggressive warfare against intemperance, against impurity, against 
dishonesty, against irreverence, against hypocrisy in all their forms. 

“Another region beyond is in the realm of a more vigorous and 
exhaustive evangelism among the young men. Although results of 
this kind have steadily increased in volume, we should not be satisfied 
with our attainments. Let us begin at once to lay such plans as will 
result in a far larger ingathering of young men into the Kingdom of 
Jesus Christ. One time when I had the privilege of conversing with 
our honoured founder Sir George Williams, I asked this question: 
“ Sir George, what was the uppermost thought in your mind, and that 
of your associates, when you were led to form this Association?” He 
said: “We had just one main thought, and that was to associate our 
efforts that we might more effectively bring to bear Christ upon the 
lives of young men.” If the one to whom God gave the initial 
impulse which called into being this movement, maintained that the 
evangelistic purpose should have right of way, we must not relegate 
it to the background. Rather let us give it a larger and more 
conspicuous place. Let anything else go rather than this. Let this 
be our consuming motive, the preaching of Christ thoroughly to all 
young men. ‘I have used the word ‘exhaustive evangelism,’ by which 
I mean preaching Christ so fully that the blood of the souls of young 
men will not rest upon our heads. 

“One of the largest unoccupied regions for us is in the realm of 
prayer. The largest talent which God has given to the Young 
Men’s Christian Association—and, by the way, the largest talent He 
has given to every Christian—is the power of prayer. What right 
have we to leave unappropriated and unapplied the mightiest force for 
the salvation of men and the energising of Christian movements. The 
Christian Church will not witness her largest triumphs until individual 
believers everywhere come to recognize more fully their priesthood 
unto God, and get into the secret places to live these great energies 
that move God, that move the world. Let us go to the secret place. 

“Yet another region beyond is in the realm of securing more 
young men to devote their lives to Christian service. We must in 
some way stop the decline in the number of strong young men enter- 
ing the Christian ministry. The Association can do this better than 


66 


any other organization with which I am familiar. We must have a 
great army of young men to go out to the non-Christian nations. I 
am looking into the faces of some young men whom God would call 
to this work, possibly to-day. Let us count it all joy that we may 
sprinkle with our lives many nations, if need be by martyrdom, that 
this gospel of Christ may be preached to every creature. Let those 
of us whom God does not call to the ministry or to the mission 
service, or the association secretaryship, resolve to make our lives 
count as laymen. What a mighty power in any community is the 
earnest and active Christian doctor, the Christian lawyer, the Chris- 
tian business man. Let us look upon the Association not only as a 
field but also and especially as a force to be wielded on behalf of the 
world’s evangelization and the establishment of the reign of Christ 
from the rivers unto the ends of the earth. 

“A word about the perils of the Association movement. I just 
mention them; pride; jealousies and divisions; leaning on the past; 
depending upon our wealth, equipment, organization and machinery; 
compromising the fundamental spiritual principles on which we rest; 
not putting first things first. I conceive these to be among our 
chief trials. Let us watch, and let him that thinketh he standeth 
take heed lest he fall. 

“What is the result of entering the regions beyond, which have 
been opened before us? The secret is the same as that which has 
made possible the achievements outlined—note it well—the uplifted 
Christ. ‘I, if I be lifted up, will draw all men unto me.’ Another 
element in the secret is yielding to the sway of the Spirit of God, for 
Christ said that greater works than He wrought should we do if we 
yielded to that sway. And if we would have the ever-enlarging results 
we must realize in experience the principle involved in the words of 
Christ—‘ Except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die, it 
abideth by itself alone but if it die, it bringeth forth much fruit.” 
The cultivation of a constant sense of vocation, that is, an ever-present 
realization that every man of us is called by God to promote this 
great work, will have very much to do with achieving the larger 
things. Responsibility in the last analysis is individual, untransfer- 
able and urgent. It is individual. God is going to judge each man 
of us by what he is and by what he does. We cannot pass this 
responsibility on to any other man. Our responsibility, let it be 
repeated, is urgent. ‘The work which centuries might have done 
must crowd the hour of setting sun.” “We must work the works of 
rape that sent me, while it is day: the night cometh when no man can 
work.’ ” 


UNVEILING THE TABLET. 


On Monday afternoon, June 10, at 3.30 o’clock, the Histori- 
cal Tablet which had been erected on the Gault Bros. Building 
on St. Helen Street was unveiled. A platform had been 
erected for invited guests of the Association, and a large 
number gathered in the street. Mr. C. T. Williams again 
presided. The thymn, “ How firm a Foundation,” was sung, 
after which Rev. Dr. McWilliams offered prayer. Mr. 


67 


Howard Williams, of London, England, was then introduced 
and spoke as follows:— 


“Mr. President, Ladies and Gentlemen: I consider it a high 
honour to be invited to take part in this memorial gathering to-day, 
and to help unveil the tablet to commemorate the introduction, or the 
formation of the Young Men’s Christian Association on the American 
continent. Your beautiful city enjoys the proud distinction of being 
the birthplace of the first Association in the New World, and it is a 
source of great satisfaction to all of us that the Association started 
here first, under the grand old flag we all love and honour. 

“In England, we have a society to mark the birthplace of our 
famous men; I do not know whether that society has a counterpart 
in this country, but I know of no better way to teach the rising gene- 
ration the great facts of national and social import than by placing a 
tablet in some conspicuous position where all who run may read. 

“Tt is impossible to recall the history of this Young Men’s Chris- 
tian Association without paying tribute to the memory of Her 
Gracious Majesty Queen Victoria, for it was one of the grand institu- 
tions (and their name was legion), inaugurated in her reign. Her 
warm sympathy for the young men of the Empire was an example of 
her devotion to the best interests of her people. The great Queen 
Mother showed special interest in the Young Men’s Christian Associa- 
tion on the occasion of our Jubilee in London a few years ago. She 
was truly a noble woman. She reigned in our hearts and helped make 
the Empire the envy, as she was the admiration, of the whole world. 
And while we mourn her loss, we thank God for the King, so well 
able to reign over us. His life has been spent in the midst of the 
people, sharing their happiness and prosperity, in ameliorating the 
condition of the lowly, and in doing what he has been able to do to 
comfort the sick and suffering. We in England owe him a debt of 
gratitude for the help he has given to the Association in the past, and 
we believe that should the occasion occur again when we require his 
help. we are bound to have it. 

“ Now, ladies and gentlemen, it is a little difficult to realize to-day 
the great change that has taken place in the conditions of service 
required by mercantile men fifty years ago. In those days the 
mercantile interests of our own country were paramount. The greed 
of money-making tempted the employer to show little consideration 
for the happiness, the safety or the health of the employee. Young 
men worked early and late, and had hardly any opportunity of 
improving their minds, or their bodies. Then came the formation of 
the Young Men’s Christian Association in London. Please under- 
stand me: I do not claim everything for the Association, but who 
could have foretold that a dozen young men working in a London 
warehouse would have formed an Association which, within half a 
century, would have girdled the world with seven thousand Associa- 
tions; would have numbered its members by hundreds of thousands, 
and owned property to the value of millions of dollars. They were 
not particularly clever young men, but they shared an enthusiasm for 
the work they had undertaken. They banded themselves together to 
promote the religious welfare of young men in similar positions in 
life. Their work was of a distinctly missionary character. It was a 
mission of young men to young men. Their motto was, ‘“ Christ for 
young men, and young men for Christ.” They taught this, that 


68 


religion was a personal matter between a young man and his God, it 
was a vital principle which did not expend itself in going to church 
on Sunday, but it was a power which must be applied to the daily 
life, and be the mainspring of every thought and action. 

“ Now, in 1851 a unique opportunity presented itself to the Associa- 
tion in London to bring the claims of a Young Men’s Christian 
Association, and its advantages, before the young men of the world. 
We had in that year the opening of the first great international 
exhibition, and thousands of people came from all parts of the world 
to visit it. The Association had written for it a large number of 
tracts and pamphlets, the bottom of each one of which contained an 
invitation to the receiver, to come to the rooms of the Association. 
A gentleman from Montreal visiting the Old Country, received one 
of these leaflets, and went to the Association, and as a result of his 
visit, on his return to Montreal, a similar Association was formed on 
the site we stand on to-day. I need not tell the history of your 
Association, for your admirable Secretary, Mr. Budge, has already 
done so in print, and you here are all familiar with that spacious 
building on Dominion Square, which is a credit to the commercial 
metropolis of Canada, and a token of the large-hearted generosity of 
your citizens. 


dialed at alta Gate

Wal 


“ Now, Ladies and Gentlemen, it is to commemorate the organiza- 
tion of this first Young Men’s Christian Association on the American 
Continent that I have now the honour, as my father’s representative, 
to unveil the tablet.” 


69 


“ Now, my friends, you will notice that the names of the original 
founders do not appear on the tablet, and I will tell you why. It is 
no secret.” It is typical of Association membership.  Self-forgetful- 
ness is one of its virtues, but although their names are not recorded 
here, we know that they were good men, true men, patriotic men, 
men with great hearts and strong faith. They knew the value of a 
Godly life, and the moral influence of Christian character, and they 
organized not merely to benefit the young fellows around them, but 
to help the stranger coming to your city. They were imbued with 
the true Imperial instinct. They realized the great future ahead for 
Canada and they foresaw that Montreal would be the gate through 
which tens of thousands, and hundreds of thousands of young men 
would pass to people your splendid country beyond, and knowing as 
they did that the future of the Dominion, for weal or for woe, depend- 
ed on the character of those young men, they instituted meetings and 
Bible classes to teach the young fellows how to live. They formed 
educational classes to enable the young man whose education had 
been neglected to meet the commercial requirements of the day. 
They played the role of guardian angel to the youngster from across 
the sea, and provided a home away from home. They gave him 
wholesome amusement, and healthy recreation. They believed in 
Christian manliness, and built a gymnasium where he could develop 
the muscles God had given him, and build up a strong constitution to 
aid him in the battle of life. If he was ill, they visited him in the 
hospital. If he was called home, they followed him to the cemetery. 
All honour, I say, to those men. Their record is a fine example ot 
Christianity in action. 

But these men did more: They promoted similar institutions in 
Toronto, Kingston, Brockville, and other cities and towns, and render- 
ed valuable services in many ways to the city, and throughout these 
long fifty years, through evil report and good report, in sunshine and 
in troublous times, the committee and officers of your Association 
have worked unceasingly. The building in Dominion Square is as 
much a monument to their energy and labour as this tablet is to the 
formation of the Association on this site, and I feel sure that so long 
as the work of the Association is carried on to the glory of God and 
for the benefit of young men the committee will never lack the 
support of the citizens of Montreal.” 


At the conclusion of Mr. Howard Williams’s address the 
Secretary announced that the following cablegram was sent. 


“June roth, 1gor. 
“ Sir George Williams, 
St. Paul’s Churchyard, London,— 
Montreal sends Jubilee greetings. Hebrews twelve, one and two.” 


“BUDGE? 


THE INFLUENCE OF THE MONTREAL ASSOCIATION. 


Mr. Joun R. Morr then spoke as follows:— 


“Mr. President, Ladies and Gentlemen: Without losing from 
thought and memory the inspiring and instructive address to which 


70 


we have just listened with much appreciation, and without attempting 
to recapitulate the sweep of the Association achievements on the 
continent as a whole, concerning which we had the privilege of 
speaking yesterday, we would at this time concentrate attention 
upon the work and influence of the Montreal Association, which is, 
as we have heard, the parent Association of the North American 
movement. 

“The Montreal Association has helped to mould the young 
manhood of this great city for well nigh two generations. In doing 
so it has, in a marked way, helped to promote the welfare and to 
determine the destiny of the city. The Montreal Association has 
combined the forces of young men of all the churches of the city, 
and brought their united influence to bear against a united opposition 
of the forces of temptation, a united indifference, a united scepticism, 
a united worldliness, and is therefore achieving, and has achieved, what 
could not have been accomplished by these young men working as 
individuals or as detachments not related to each other. 

“The Montreal Association, let me add, has commanded and kept 
the confidence of the churches throughout the city through all these 
years, and that in itself is a testimony of which the Association may 
well be proud. Moreover, it has inspired increasingly, the backing 
and co-operation in money and time, of the business and professional 
men of the city. During these fifty years, they have counted it a 
privilege to place at the disposal of this Association not less than half 
a million of dollars, and it is interesting to notice that they seem to 
have the disposition to increase the amount from year to year. While 
wisely conservative, the Montreal Association has been truly progres- 
sive, and has, step by step, incorporated the best ideas wrought out 
and evolved in the rich and varied experience of the entire Association 
Brotherhood. They have been trying all things, and holding fast at the 
saine time to that which is good. While the progress in things external 
and material has been nothing less than remarkable, the Montreal 
Association has preserved an ever-spreading spiritual life. This is 
not an easy thing todo. Moreover, the Montreal Association has been 
unswervingly loyal to the central points of the Christian faith. There 
has never been the slightest suspicion, or the least question with 
reference to the position of this organization upon the things essen- 
tial, and which we believe. The leaders of this work have insisted by 
example and by word, on the supremacy of the religious work of the 
Young Men’s Christian Association. Thank God for their example, 
and for their influence in this respect. One unbroken line of conver- 
sions is the answer which God has afforded them for their loyalty in 
these essential things. They have constantly emphasized the study 
of the Word of God, and have not lost sight of the true objective of 
all Bible study, namely, character and service. The Montreal Associa- 
tion has stood for developing and sending out young men of reality. 
These young men as they go into athletics and other sports, stand for 
that which is honourable and clean and wholesome. As they go into 
society they stand for good comradeship, for Christian friendship, and 
for purity. They go into business, not to become tricksters, but men 
of integrity and of sterling honour. They devote themselves to the 
legal and medical professions, not to become pettifoggers and quacks, 
but to honour the best traditions of these great professions. They 
enter the service of their country not to become merely politicians, 


71 


but statesmen. They participate in the activities of the Church, not as 
hypocrites, but as men of reality. This spirit of genuineness, of 
sincerity, is one of the deep secrets of the achievements of the Mont- 
real Association. Emerson says, “What you are, speaks so loud that 
I cannot hear what you say.” One thinks of this in thinking of that 
true note ever sounded out in silence as it were, by the lives lived and 
developed in this Association. 

“The Montreal Association has been, and is, a great training 
school. It has sent out into the Christian ministry of different 
denominations, into the foreign mission field, and into the secretary- 
ship of the Associations not less than forty young men. This is a 
mighty work in itself. But besides this, it has trained and inspired 
hundreds, I think I may say thousands, of men who have scattered 
themselves among the scores of churches in the city, and are to-day 
true pillars of the Church and more efficient workmen as a result of 
the training and inspiration afforded by the Association. While intent 
upon building up the young manhood of Montreal, this Association 
has been a formative factor in the Association movement throughout 
the Dominion of Canada, and has helped greatly to hold the Associa- 
tions of the States to the true purpose of the Young Mer ’s Christian 
Association. 

* The Montreal Association, moreover, has included within the 
range of its sympathy and helpfulness, the young men of the whole 
world. This Association has esteemed it an honour to recognize 
itself as a part of the world-wide Association movement. The Creed 
of St. Augustine might fitly be quoted to-day to characterize the work 
of this Association, and its position : ‘* A whole Christ for my salva- 
tion, a whole Bible for my staff, a whole Church for my fellowship, 
and a whole world for my parish.’ The Christian Association, like 
the Christian individual, cannot live unto itself. This Association 
early recognized, and it has never ceased to emphasize that it has a 
mission to the young men of less favored lands. Therefore, I am able 
to say now what it gives me great pleasure to say, that the Montreal 
Association is doing more, and has done more, than any other Asso- 
ciation on this continent, or any other continent, to extend the helpful 
influence of the Association brotherhood to the non-Christian world. 
I might almost say that the sun never sets on the activities of the 
Montreal Young Men’s Christian Association, because I am reminded 
that in the Punjaub is one man, in Bengal another, in the Madras Presi- 
dency a third, travelling among the cities of India a fourth, among the 
universities of India a fifth, in the great city of Tien-Tsin, in China, a 
sixth, and there is still a seventh in Japan. All these seven men are 
the representatives of this Association. I call attention to this record 
as an example and stimulus to other Associations and to inspire us all 
to larger achievements, because, believe me brothers, if we are to do 
the fair thing by the world for which Jesus Christ died, the Montreal 
Association must not be satisfied with what it is doing, and the other 
cities of the world must rise in their might and do much more. 

“In a word, the Montreal Association may be termed as nearly as 
we can term any association, a model Young Men’s Christian Associa- 
tion. Without flattery to Montreal, and without apologizing to any 
other Associations, because I am willing that they shall know what I 
say, but in recognition of what God hath wrought I simply state this 
as a fact. When the Foreign Department of the International Com- 


re 
(4 


mittee wish to send out a new secretary to a non-Christian nation, and 
wish to have him receive further training and instruction, and to study 
some model or type which he can reproduce in the non-Christian 
world, where do you think we send that man ? We send him to 
Montreal. 

“ Now in view of what I have stated, it is not necessary that I 
should speak of what the Montreal Association ought to be in the 
next fifty years. This Association has to be congratulated upon the 
leadership it has had in its secretaries and laymen. Keep up the high 
standard of the personnel in these two respects and continue the work 
on these lines which have been opened up by the Spirit of God, and 
there is no reason why the next fifty years of the Association should 
not be richer and yield a more abundant fruitage than the half century 
which we commemorate to-day. To this end, and this is the special 
message I would bring to-day, let us keep Jesus Christ at the centre 
of this work. We bear His name and sign. We go to Him to learn 
those methods which in the true sense of the word succeed. He 
furnishes us the ideal that moves men. We go to Him to catch that 
spirit that literally overcomes the world. We draw from Him our life. 
Anchored to Christ the work of the Montreal Association will abide, 
and only so. I congratulate the men and women of this city who 
give time and money, and energy, and influence, and active thought 
to the work of the Young Men’s Christian Association, because, 
believe me, you expend your time, and money, and energy, and 
influence, and thought upon that which will abide. After the Associa- 
tion building on Victoria Square, and after the one on Dominion 
Square, have crumbled to the dust; after this tablet has been obliterat- 
ed by the sure and tireless and never-ending work of time; after the 
prophecies of these three days have been fulfilled, so far as they have 
been in harmony with the will of God; after tongues have ceased; after 
knowledge has been done away by larger restatements of knowledge; 
after yon mountain has gone to the plain——for your own honoured 
Sir William Dawson maintained it was but the type of evanescence; 
after the beautiful St. Lawrence has ceased to run to the sea; yes, 
after this fair city gives way to that holy city, the new Jerusalem let 
down from God out of heaven, these influences, all anchored to Christ, 
will abide, for the simple reason that the world passeih away, and the 
fashion thereof, but he that doeth the will of God abideth forever, 
and for the deeper reason that Christ Himself is the same yesterday, 
to-day, yea, and forever.” 


The hymn, “ Blest be the tie that binds,” was sung, also the 
National Anthem. 

At six o’clock a luncheon was tendered the visiting dele- 
gates by the Board of Directors, succeeded by an informal 
reception of the Association members. The visitors left for 
the Jubilee Convention at Boston on the nine o'clock train.
